Furthermore, predicted unconventional SC properties such as scanning tunneling spectra of La$_{0.8}$Sr$_{0.2}$NiO$_2$ and Pr$_{0.8}$Sr$_{0.2}$NiO$_2$ are ready for immediate experimental verifications.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a fully ab initio theoretical study of superconductivity in optimally doped infinite-layer nickelates Re0.8Sr0.2NiO2 (Re=La, Pr, Nd), treating electron-phonon coupling, screened Coulomb repulsion, and spin fluctuations on equal footing within density functional theory for superconductors. The authors find these materials are two-band superconductors with sign-reversing d_{x^2-y^2}-wave gap functions, and demonstrate that spin fluctuations—not phonons—drive the superconductivity, with T_c becoming negligibly small (~0.01 K) when spin fluctuations are turned off.
AI.motivation: Infinite-layer nickelates have emerged as a new family of potential unconventional high-Tc superconductors, but fundamental questions about their superconducting pairing mechanism and gap symmetry remain unresolved. A fully ab initio study treating all relevant pairing channels on equal footing is needed to settle these debates.
AI.method: The authors performed ab initio density functional theory for superconductors (SCDFT) calculations, incorporating electron-phonon coupling (EPC), screened Coulomb repulsion, and spin fluctuation (SF) interactions on an equal footing for optimally doped Re0.8Sr0.2NiO2 (Re=La, Pr, Nd). They computed Fermi surfaces, superconducting gap functions, critical temperatures, and quasiparticle density of states, and analyzed the Lindhard response function to trace the origin of the gap structure.
AI.result: The materials are found to be two-band superconductors with sign-reversing d_{x^2-y^2}(±)-wave gaps on different Fermi surface pockets. When SF interaction is turned off, T_c drops to ~0.01 K, proving SF-mediated superconductivity. SF interaction is an order of magnitude stronger than EPC and Coulomb repulsion on the large quasi-2D Fermi surface pocket at the BZ center, while EPC dominates on the small 3D electron pockets at BZ corners. Nodal gap structure arises from peaks in the Lindhard response at BZ corners. Calculated properties agree with most experiments, and predicted STM spectra for La and Pr compounds await verification.
AI.conclusion: The superconductivity in infinite-layer nickelates Re0.8Sr0.2NiO2 is driven by spin fluctuations, leading to a nodal d_{x^2-y^2}(±)-wave pairing state, with phonons playing a secondary role on the three-dimensional Fermi pockets. The calculated results are broadly consistent with experiments, and the predicted unconventional SC properties provide testable signatures for future experimental verification.

title: Lossless Compression Performance for PETRA III Datasets
summary: Large-scale research facilities increasingly face the challenge of managing rapidly growing data volumes while maintaining sustainable archival infrastructures. We present the first comprehensive study of data heterogeneity and lossless general-purpose compression performance for representative datasets from the PETRA III synchrotron radiation source. Our corpus comprises more than 212 TiB of raw and processed data from ten experiments spanning multiple beamlines, detector systems, and scientific workflows. We observe substantial heterogeneity both between and within experiments, resulting in compression ratios that vary by more than two orders of magnitude across datasets. Evaluating nine widely used lossless compression tools, we find that Zstandard and LZ4 consistently occupy the high-throughput region of the Pareto front, whereas ZPAQ achieves the highest compression ratios. Furthermore, heterogeneous compression strategies that adapt compressor choice to the underlying file category outperform uniform compression policies. Extrapolating from the benchmarked datasets to the full PETRA III non-tape storage system, we estimate achievable compression ratios ranging from approximately 1.6 at $\sim$900 MiB/s throughput to 2.1 at $\sim$2 MiB/s. These results provide a quantitative basis for future archival and storage decisions at PETRA III, its future successor, PETRA IV, and other large-scale scientific facilities.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a comprehensive study of data heterogeneity and lossless compression performance on over 212 TiB of data from ten experiments at PETRA III synchrotron. It evaluates nine compression tools, finding Zstandard and LZ4 dominate the high-throughput Pareto front, ZPAQ achieves best ratios, and heterogeneous (per-file-category) compression strategies outperform uniform policies. Extrapolation to full storage estimates achievable ratios from 1.6 at ~900 MiB/s to 2.1 at ~2 MiB/s.
AI.motivation: Large-scale research facilities face rapidly growing data volumes while needing sustainable archival infrastructures. There is a lack of quantitative understanding of data heterogeneity and compression performance specific to synchrotron radiation source datasets, which is needed to inform storage and archival decisions.
AI.method: The authors assembled a corpus of over 212 TiB of raw and processed data from ten experiments across multiple beamlines, detector systems, and scientific workflows at PETRA III. They benchmarked nine widely used lossless compression tools and evaluated uniform vs. heterogeneous compression strategies that adapt compressor choice to file category.
AI.result: Compression ratios vary by more than two orders of magnitude due to heterogeneity between and within experiments. Zstandard and LZ4 consistently occupy the high-throughput region of the Pareto front, while ZPAQ achieves the highest compression ratios. Heterogeneous compression strategies outperform uniform policies. Extrapolation to full PETRA III non-tape storage estimates compression ratios from ~1.6 at ~900 MiB/s to ~2.1 at ~2 MiB/s.
AI.conclusion: The findings provide a quantitative basis for future archival and storage decisions at PETRA III, its successor PETRA IV, and other large-scale scientific facilities, demonstrating that adaptive, file-category-aware compression strategies yield better trade-offs between space savings and throughput.

title: Anomalous enhancement of thermal radiation transport by quasidisorder
summary: The transition from order to disorder is conventionally regarded as detrimental to solid-state heat transfer in classical wave and quasiparticle systems. In striking contrast, we show that in near-field thermal radiation, breaking long-range order-shifting from periodic to quasiperiodic configurations-induces a counterintuitive enhancement of energy transport. This effect arises from delocalized interactions within quasiperiodic elements, where this quasiperiodicity relays and amplifies thermal electromagnetic energy transfer across large spatial separations, surpassing even corresponding near-field scenarios. The extraordinary transport properties induced by quasidisorder effect of near-field thermal radiation could unlock exciting opportunities for heat flow manipulation, offering transformative implications for thermal science and advancing the fundamental understanding of collective excitations in non-ordered systems.

AI.tldr: This paper reveals a counterintuitive phenomenon where breaking long-range order (shifting from periodic to quasiperiodic configurations) enhances near-field thermal radiation transport, contrary to the conventional view that disorder harms solid-state heat transfer. This "quasidisorder effect" enables delocalized interactions that relay and amplify thermal electromagnetic energy over large spatial separations, even surpassing corresponding near-field scenarios.
AI.motivation: Conventional wisdom holds that transitioning from order to disorder degrades solid-state heat transfer in classical wave and quasiparticle systems. The authors challenge this assumption by investigating whether breaking long-range order could instead enhance energy transport in near-field thermal radiation.
AI.method: The study examines near-field thermal radiation in quasiperiodic configurations, comparing them against periodic and corresponding near-field scenarios. The analysis focuses on delocalized interactions within quasiperiodic elements as the mechanism for enhanced electromagnetic energy transfer.
AI.result: Shifting from periodic to quasiperiodic configurations induces a counterintuitive enhancement of energy transport in near-field thermal radiation. This quasidisorder effect relays and amplifies thermal electromagnetic energy transfer across large spatial separations, exceeding even corresponding near-field scenarios.
AI.conclusion: The quasidisorder effect in near-field thermal radiation offers transformative opportunities for heat flow manipulation, with implications for thermal science and advancing fundamental understanding of collective excitations in non-ordered systems.

title: Spin-orbit-entangled frustrated magnetism in fcc Ba$_2$(Yb,Nd)NbO$_6$ double perovskites
summary: The search for candidate Kitaev materials has largely focused on 4$d$ and 5$d$ transition-metal compounds with various lattice geometries. In contrast, investigations of rare-earth 4$f$ systems have thus far been restricted mainly to honeycomb and triangular lattices. In this work, we investigate the rare-earth-based double perovskites Ba$_2$YbNbO$_6$ and Ba$_2$NdNbO$_6$, which crystallize in a face-centered cubic structure. Magnetization and heat-capacity measurements establish isolated ${j_{\rm eff}} = 1/2$ Kramers doublet ground states arising from strong spin-orbit coupling (SOC) and crystal electric-field effects, which are further supported by density-functional theory calculations. Millikelvin-temperature thermodynamic measurements reveal long-range magnetic order with moderate frustration in both compounds. The emergence of magnetic order may be understood within an order-by-disorder scenario, as theoretically proposed for rare-earth fcc lattices with finite Kitaev interactions. Our results thus identify Ba$_2$YbNbO$_6$ and Ba$_2$NdNbO$_6$ as promising rare-earth spin-orbit-entangled magnets and motivate further experimental and theoretical investigations aimed at determining the complete exchange tensor to elucidate the microscopic origin of the underlying magnetic interactions.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates rare-earth-based double perovskites Ba₂YbNbO₆ and Ba₂NdNbO₆, which crystallize in a face-centered cubic structure. Through magnetization and heat-capacity measurements supported by DFT calculations, they establish isolated j_eff = 1/2 Kramers doublet ground states arising from strong spin-orbit coupling and crystal electric-field effects. Millikelvin thermodynamic measurements reveal long-range magnetic order with moderate frustration, potentially understood via an order-by-disorder scenario proposed for rare-earth fcc lattices with finite Kitaev interactions.
AI.motivation: The search for Kitaev materials has focused almost exclusively on 4d/5d transition-metal systems, while rare-earth 4f systems have only been explored on honeycomb and triangular lattices. This work aims to expand rare-earth Kitaev candidate materials to face-centered cubic lattice geometries by investigating double perovskites, motivated by the theoretical proposal that rare-earth fcc lattices with finite Kitaev interactions may exhibit novel magnetic order.
AI.method: The authors performed magnetization and heat-capacity measurements on Ba₂YbNbO₆ and Ba₂NdNbO₆, including millikelvin-temperature thermodynamic measurements to probe magnetic ordering. These experimental results were supported by density-functional theory (DFT) calculations to confirm the electronic ground state structure.
AI.result: Both compounds exhibit isolated j_eff = 1/2 Kramers doublet ground states arising from strong spin-orbit coupling and crystal electric-field effects. Millikelvin-temperature measurements reveal long-range magnetic order with moderate frustration in both compounds. The observed magnetic order can be understood within an order-by-disorder scenario as theoretically proposed for rare-earth fcc lattices with finite Kitaev interactions.
AI.conclusion: The results identify Ba₂YbNbO₆ and Ba₂NdNbO₆ as promising rare-earth spin-orbit-entangled magnets. The work motivates further experimental and theoretical investigations to determine the complete exchange tensor and elucidate the microscopic origin of the underlying magnetic interactions in these fcc-lattice rare-earth systems.

title: Skyrmion Excitations in the $ν=-1$ Quantum Hall state in Monolayer Graphene
summary: We investigate the skyrmion excited states atop the $SU(4)$ quantum Hall ferromagnetic ground state at filling factor $ν=-1$ in monolayer graphene. The competition among short-range anisotropic interactions, the Zeeman coupling, and sublattice symmetry-breaking potential gives rise to four distinct spin-valley-ordered ground-state phases. Combining effective field theory with the Hartree--Fock approximation, we develop a variational framework that incorporates both the long-range Coulomb interaction and the symmetry-breaking terms on an equal footing. Variational minimization determines the optimal skyrmion texture, including both its spatial radial profile and internal $SU(4)$ spinor structure. We establish the phase diagram of skyrmion excitations, identify thirteen distinct skyrmion phases under different external-field conditions, and determine their spin-valley textures, energies, and characteristic sizes. The robustness of the results against different radial ansätze demonstrates the reliability of our variational approach. Our work provides a systematic framework for studying skyrmion excitations in multicomponent quantum Hall ferromagnets and can be naturally extended to more general $SU(4)$ quantum Hall systems.

AI.tldr: This paper studies skyrmion excited states in monolayer graphene at filling factor ν=-1 atop an SU(4) quantum Hall ferromagnetic ground state. Using a variational framework combining effective field theory and Hartree-Fock approximation, the authors identify four distinct ground-state phases and map out a phase diagram of skyrmion excitations featuring thirteen distinct phases with different spin-valley textures, energies, and sizes, validated against multiple radial ansätze.
AI.motivation: To understand and systematically characterize skyrmion excitations in multicomponent quantum Hall ferromagnets in graphene, where the interplay of short-range anisotropic interactions, Zeeman coupling, and sublattice symmetry-breaking potential creates complex competing ground states and their corresponding topological excitations.
AI.method: The authors combine effective field theory with the Hartree-Fock approximation to build a variational framework that treats long-range Coulomb interaction and symmetry-breaking terms equally. Variational minimization determines the optimal skyrmion texture—both its spatial radial profile and internal SU(4) spinor structure.
AI.result: The work establishes a phase diagram of skyrmion excitations with thirteen distinct skyrmion phases under different external-field conditions, determining their spin-valley textures, energies, and characteristic sizes. The results are robust against different radial ansätze, confirming the reliability of the variational approach.
AI.conclusion: This work provides a systematic framework for studying skyrmion excitations in multicomponent quantum Hall ferromagnets that can be naturally extended to more general SU(4) quantum Hall systems, offering predictive capability for experimentally relevant observables.

title: Measurement and control of the interaction frequency shift in bosonic optical lattice clocks
summary: We report precise measurements of inter-level interactions in a bosonic optical lattice clock based on $^{88}$Sr atoms. We observe a nonlinear density dependence of the clock shift, even without reaching quantum degeneracy. In a 2D lattice, the Rabi line shape exhibits an interaction sideband consistent with a collective spin model, while in a 1D lattice the shift is modified by density-induced dephasing. These findings, combined with a careful choice of interrogation detuning and atomic density, can enable operation at a net-zero systematic density shift in $^{88}$Sr lattice clocks. We discuss the implications of these findings in many-body physics, quantum simulation, and precision isotope shift measurements, which provide a powerful probe for new physics beyond the Standard Model.

AI.tldr: This paper reports precise measurements of inter-level interactions in a bosonic optical lattice clock based on 88Sr atoms, observing a nonlinear density dependence of the clock shift even without quantum degeneracy. The study reveals an interaction sideband in 2D lattices consistent with a collective spin model and density-induced dephasing in 1D lattices, enabling net-zero systematic density shift operation.
AI.motivation: To provide precise measurements of inter-level interactions in a bosonic optical lattice clock and understand the nonlinear density-dependent clock shifts, which are crucial for accurate clock operation and for exploring many-body physics and precision isotope shift measurements.
AI.method: The authors use a bosonic optical lattice clock based on 88Sr atoms and measure inter-level interactions in both 2D and 1D lattice configurations. They observe Rabi line shapes with interaction sidebands in 2D lattices, which are compared with a collective spin model, and study density-induced dephasing effects in 1D lattices.
AI.result: A nonlinear density dependence of the clock shift was observed without reaching quantum degeneracy. In 2D lattices, the Rabi line shape exhibited an interaction sideband consistent with a collective spin model, while in 1D lattices the shift was modified by density-induced dephasing. These insights enable operation at a net-zero systematic density shift.
AI.conclusion: The findings enable operation at net-zero systematic density shift in 88Sr lattice clocks and have implications for many-body physics, quantum simulation, and precision isotope shift measurements, providing a powerful probe for new physics beyond the Standard Model.

title: Post-Collision Thermal Excitation and Survival-Limited Cluster Growth in the Gas Phase
summary: Gas-phase cluster growth by monomer addition is commonly modeled as an isothermal process. We develop a survival-limited framework in which association produces a thermally excited cluster that may dissociate before either cooling through bath-gas collisions or encountering the next monomer. A continuous-energy survival probability is first derived for an individual post-association thermal trajectory and is then marginalized over distributions of excitation energy, equilibrium energy, and monomer-arrival time using a trajectory functional. Molecular-dynamics simulations of water, silver, and gold clusters provide size-dependent caloric relationships and latent heats, while event-based Monte Carlo simulations independently test the survival formulation. Theory and Monte Carlo results agree closely. The ensemble-averaged survival probability exhibits strong and non-monotonic size dependence, with the largest thermal penalties generally occurring for the smallest clusters. Intermediate-size local maxima arise only when complete cluster-energy distributions are retained and result from competition between curvature-enhanced dissociation and the narrowing of the low-energy tail with increasing size. Surviving clusters are consequently drawn preferentially from the colder portion of the pre-collision energy distribution, and mean thermal trajectories can substantially underestimate population survival. To connect single-event survival to cumulative growth, we introduce a thermal forward-rate correction relative to an isothermal reference and incorporate it into a reversible birth--death model. Although the correction at each size may be moderate, its multiplicative accumulation can increase mean first-passage times by many orders of magnitude. The framework provides a general route for identifying post-collision stabilization as a control on gas-phase cluster growth.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a survival-limited framework for gas-phase cluster growth where monomer addition produces thermally excited clusters that may dissociate before cooling or encountering the next monomer. The framework derives a continuous-energy survival probability marginalized over energy and arrival-time distributions, validated against molecular dynamics and Monte Carlo simulations of water, silver, and gold clusters. Survival probabilities show strong, non-monotonic size dependence, and a thermal forward-rate correction incorporated into a reversible birth-death model can increase mean first-passage times by orders of magnitude.
AI.motivation: Gas-phase cluster growth by monomer addition is typically modeled as isothermal, which ignores the thermal excitation and possible dissociation following association events. This work aims to account for post-collision stabilization as a key control on cluster growth.
AI.method: The authors derive a continuous-energy survival probability for individual post-association thermal trajectories, marginalized over excitation-energy, equilibrium-energy, and monomer-arrival-time distributions via a trajectory functional. Molecular dynamics simulations of water, silver, and gold clusters supply size-dependent caloric relationships and latent heats, while event-based Monte Carlo simulations independently test the survival formulation.
AI.result: Theory and Monte Carlo results agree closely. The ensemble-averaged survival probability exhibits strong, non-monotonic size dependence, with largest thermal penalties for the smallest clusters. Intermediate-size local maxima arise only when full cluster-energy distributions are retained, from competition between curvature-enhanced dissociation and narrowing of the low-energy tail. Surviving clusters are preferentially drawn from the colder portion of the pre-collision distribution. A thermal forward-rate correction is introduced; while the per-size correction may be moderate, its multiplicative accumulation can raise mean first-passage times by many orders of magnitude.
AI.conclusion: The survival-limited framework provides a general route for identifying post-collision stabilization as a control on gas-phase cluster growth, demonstrating that non-isothermal effects can dramatically impact cumulative growth kinetics.

title: Machine-Learning-Accelerated Metallene Stabilization from High-Throughput Sandwich Modeling
summary: Metallenes have appealing properties, but stabilizing them in a monolayer phase poses challenges for their synthesis. A recent experiment showed that the van der Waals squeezing method can stabilize certain metallenes in a MoS2 sandwich. This pioneering work motivates systematic studies, but such studies are experimentally impractical, while first-principles modeling remains prohibitive. Here, armed with universal machine-learning interatomic potentials, we constructed 1620 metallene sandwich heterostructures containing 6 different sandwich layers and 45 metals. We performed phonon calculations, which revealed 1208 dynamically stable structures. We found that transition-metal dichalcogenides, particularly MoSe2, are highly effective in stabilizing metallenes. Specifically, buckled hexagonal and honeycomb crystal lattices exhibit the greatest stability. We further evaluated the thermal stability of selected heterostructures with density-functional theory molecular dynamics simulations at room temperature. By uncovering the physical and chemical factors governing the stabilization of metallenes, our results provide systematic insights to guide and accelerate synthesis for future applications.

AI.tldr: This paper uses universal machine-learning interatomic potentials to systematically screen 1620 metallene sandwich heterostructures, identifying 1208 dynamically stable configurations and revealing that transition-metal dichalcogenides, especially MoSe2, are highly effective stabilizers for metallenes, with buckled hexagonal and honeycomb lattices being most stable.
AI.motivation: Metallenes have appealing properties but stabilizing them in a monolayer phase is challenging. A recent experiment demonstrated that van der Waals squeezing can stabilize metallenes in MoS2 sandwiches, motivating systematic studies that are experimentally impractical and prohibitively expensive for first-principles calculations.
AI.method: The authors constructed 1620 metallene sandwich heterostructures using universal machine-learning interatomic potentials, combining 6 different sandwich layers and 45 metals. They performed phonon calculations to assess dynamic stability and used density-functional theory molecular dynamics simulations to evaluate thermal stability of selected heterostructures at room temperature.
AI.result: Phonon calculations revealed 1208 dynamically stable structures. Transition-metal dichalcogenides, particularly MoSe2, were highly effective stabilizers. Buckled hexagonal and honeycomb crystal lattices exhibited the greatest stability.
AI.conclusion: By identifying the physical and chemical factors governing metallene stabilization in sandwich heterostructures, the results provide systematic insights to guide and accelerate future synthesis of metallenes for applications.

title: Predictive Formulas for Scattering Mean Free Path for General Disordered Dielectric Media Beyond the Long-Wavelength Regime
comment: 22 pages, 8+3 figures, one supplementary document and one supplementary data set
summary: We derive predictive formulas for the scattering mean free path $\ell_s$ of statistically homogeneous two-phase dielectric media in dimensions $d=1,2,3$. Unlike Mie-based estimates limited to identical circular or spherical scatterers, the formulas apply to arbitrarily shaped and polydisperse particulate media as well as nonparticulate media, with microstructure entering through the spectral density. The formulas are based on the exact strong-contrast expansion for the effective dynamic dielectric constant. We apply them to five nonhyperuniform and hyperuniform models and validate selected cases using finite-difference time-domain simulations. For $k_1/s \lesssim 1$, where $k_1$ is the incident wavenumber and $s$ is the specific surface, the predictions agree well with simulations and are consistent with Mie theory where applicable, while improving accuracy for two-dimensional transverse-magnetic polarization. Mie estimates become more accurate for $k_1/s \gtrsim 1$. For hyperuniform media with $\widetildeχ_V(k)\sim k^α$ at small $k$, the theory predicts $\ell_s\sim k_1^{-(d+1+α)}$; stealthy hyperuniform media are transparent over a finite wavenumber interval. These results provide a microstructure-based route to predict and design wave transport in general disordered dielectric materials.

AI.tldr: The paper derives predictive formulas for the scattering mean free path (ℓ_s) of statistically homogeneous two-phase dielectric media in d=1,2,3 dimensions, applicable to arbitrarily shaped, polydisperse particulate media and nonparticulate media via the spectral density. Based on the strong-contrast expansion for the effective dynamic dielectric constant, the formulas are validated against FDTD simulations on five hyperuniform/nonhyperuniform models and show scaling ℓ_s ~ k_1^{-(d+1+α)} for hyperuniform media with spectral-density exponent α.
AI.motivation: Existing Mie-based estimates are limited to identical circular or spherical scatterers. A general microstructure-based approach is needed to predict wave transport (scattering mean free path) in arbitrarily shaped and polydisperse disordered dielectric media.
AI.method: The authors use the exact strong-contrast expansion for the effective dynamic dielectric constant to derive closed-form predictive formulas for ℓ_s in d=1,2,3, where microstructure enters through the spectral density. The formulas are applied to five hyperuniform and nonhyperuniform models and validated with finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) simulations.
AI.result: For k_1/s ≲ 1 (small wavenumber relative to specific surface), the predictions agree well with simulations and are consistent with Mie theory where applicable, with improved accuracy for 2D transverse-magnetic polarization. Mie estimates become more accurate for k_1/s ≳ 1. For hyperuniform media with spectral density scaling χ̃_V(k)~k^α at small k, ℓ_s ~ k_1^{-(d+1+α)}, and stealthy hyperuniform media are transparent over a finite wavenumber interval.
AI.conclusion: The derived formulas provide a microstructure-based route to predict and engineer wave transport in general disordered dielectric materials, extending beyond Mie-theory limitations and revealing novel transparency behavior in stealthy hyperuniform media.

title: Evidence for superconductivity at 190 K in a pressure-overdoped cuprate
summary: It is well established that the critical temperature ($T_c$) of cuprate superconductors can be tuned by pressure. For example, compression decouples the hole doping from chemical doping allowing for overdoped samples far beyond what is possible at ambient pressure. In this work, multiple techniques are used to probe the onset of the Meissner effect at $T_c$ as a function of pressure in $\mathrm{Pb_{0.4}Bi_{1.6}Sr_2Ca_2Cu_3O_{10+δ}}$ (Bi-2223) to 60 GPa in different compression environments. Samples compressed under quasihydrostatic conditions exhibit a distinctive non-monotonic pressure dependence of $T_c$ below 25 GPa, in agreement with previous reports. With further increase in pressure $T_c$ climbs continuously to 190 K at 60 GPa. Evidence for critical temperatures exceeding those reported to date for cuprates at ambient and high pressures, the results may be understood in terms of the proposed second superconducting regime at high hole doping.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the pressure dependence of the superconducting critical temperature (Tc) in the cuprate superconductor Pb0.4Bi1.6Sr2Ca2Cu3O10+δ (Bi-2223) up to 60 GPa under different compression conditions. Quasihydrostatic compression reveals a non-monotonic Tc behavior below 25 GPa, followed by a continuous rise to 190 K at 60 GPa—exceeding previously reported cuprate critical temperatures—which is interpreted as evidence for a second superconducting regime at high hole doping.
AI.motivation: To explore how pressure tunes the critical temperature of cuprate superconductors, particularly to access overdoped regimes beyond what is possible at ambient pressure, and to search for enhanced superconductivity beyond previously known limits.
AI.method: Multiple probing techniques were used to detect the onset of the Meissner effect at Tc as a function of pressure in Bi-2223 samples up to 60 GPa, comparing different compression environments (quasihydrostatic and other conditions).
AI.result: Quasihydrostatically compressed samples show a distinctive non-monotonic Tc pressure dependence below 25 GPa, consistent with earlier reports. Above that, Tc continuously increases to 190 K at 60 GPa, exceeding critical temperatures previously reported for cuprates at both ambient and high pressures.
AI.conclusion: The observed record-high Tc values support the concept of a second superconducting regime at high hole doping in cuprates, enabled by pressure decoupling hole doping from chemical doping.

title: Uncertainty-guided active learning for surrogate prediction of stream-finishing wear fields
summary: In stream finishing, the wear experienced by a workpiece depends strongly on its orientation within the rotating abrasive media. Determining suitable orientations to achieve uniform wear requires evaluating the wear-rate field over all feasible orientations. Although the discrete element method (DEM) accurately resolves particle interactions, simulating hundreds of feasible orientations for a new geometry is computationally expensive. We present an uncertainty-guided surrogate framework that predicts, directly from geometry, the three fields governing erosion: per-triangle normal impact velocity, tangential impact velocity, and particle impact flux. These fields are combined through the Finnie wear model to reconstruct the wear-rate distribution. The surrogate employs a deep ensemble whose disagreement estimates epistemic uncertainty, enabling an active-learning strategy that selectively performs DEM simulations for the most uncertain orientations. Trained using only $13\%$ of the $696$ feasible orientations, the surrogate achieves Spearman rank correlations of $0.93$, $0.89$, and $0.93$ for the normal impact velocity, tangential impact velocity, and particle impact flux, respectively. Moreover, the predicted uncertainty is well calibrated, reliably anticipating prediction error and the fidelity of the reconstructed wear field, which matches DEM with a Spearman rank correlation of up to $0.97$ for low-uncertainty orientations and degrades in a controlled manner as uncertainty increases.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an uncertainty-guided surrogate framework that predicts the three fields governing erosion in stream finishing (normal impact velocity, tangential impact velocity, and particle impact flux) directly from geometry, using a deep ensemble with active learning to selectively perform expensive DEM simulations. Trained on only 13% of feasible orientations, it achieves Spearman correlations of 0.89-0.93 for the fields and up to 0.97 for reconstructed wear, with well-calibrated uncertainty estimates.
AI.motivation: In stream finishing, workpiece wear depends strongly on orientation within rotating abrasive media, and determining suitable orientations for uniform wear requires evaluating wear-rate over all feasible orientations. While DEM accurately resolves particle interactions, simulating hundreds of orientations for a new geometry is computationally prohibitive.
AI.method: The authors develop a surrogate model based on a deep ensemble that predicts three per-triangle fields directly from geometry: normal impact velocity, tangential impact velocity, and particle impact flux. These fields are combined via the Finnie wear model to reconstruct wear-rate distribution. The deep ensemble's disagreement estimates epistemic uncertainty, enabling an active-learning strategy that selectively runs DEM simulations only for the most uncertain orientations.
AI.result: Trained on only 13% of the 696 feasible orientations, the surrogate achieves Spearman rank correlations of 0.93, 0.89, and 0.93 for normal impact velocity, tangential impact velocity, and particle impact flux respectively. The reconstructed wear field matches DEM with Spearman rank correlation up to 0.97 for low-uncertainty orientations, degrading in a controlled manner with increasing uncertainty. The predicted uncertainty is well calibrated.
AI.conclusion: The uncertainty-guided surrogate framework provides an efficient and reliable way to predict wear-rate fields in stream finishing without exhaustively running expensive DEM simulations, with calibrated uncertainty that reliably anticipates prediction error and wear-field fidelity.

title: Topological Rainbow Trapping for Spatial-frequency Demultiplexing of Underwater Acoustic Signals
summary: Efficient separation and localization of multifrequency acoustic waves are essential for underwater target recognition and acoustic energy harvesting. The underwater implementation of topological rainbow trapping remains challenging because of complex fluid-solid interactions and the difficulty of integrating long-range transport with frequency-selective localization in an open system. Here, we theoretically develop and experimentally demonstrate two underwater spatial-frequency demultiplexing mechanisms based on the acoustic analogues of the QVHE and QSHE. Both mechanisms employ SSAWs, whose fields are confined near a structured surface and decay evanescently into the surrounding water, enabling experiments without an enclosed waveguide. In the QVHE mechanism, a spatial gradient along a valley-Hall edge channel shifts the local edge-state dispersion, causing different frequency components to become localized at distinct positions and thereby realizing spectral and spatial demultiplexing. In the QSHE mechanism, one-dimensional topological edge states are coupled to frequency-selective zero-dimensional higher-order corner states. Multifrequency signals first propagate robustly along a common boundary and are then transferred to prescribed remote corners according to frequency, producing a transport-then-confinement process. This mechanism combines defect-tolerant edge transport, frequency-selective corner localization, and remote rainbow trapping. Numerical simulations and experiments verify the frequency-dependent localization and the persistence of the designed transport pathways in the presence of structural defects. The proposed open SSAW platform performs robust frequency demultiplexing at the physical layer, reducing reliance on digital signal processing and offering potential for underwater target recognition and frequency-selective acoustic energy harvesting.

AI.tldr: This paper theoretically and experimentally demonstrates two underwater spatial-frequency demultiplexing mechanisms based on quantum valley Hall effect (QVHE) and quantum spin Hall effect (QSHE) analogues, using structured surface acoustic waves (SSAWs). These open platforms enable frequency-selective localization, defect-tolerant edge transport, and remote rainbow trapping without enclosed waveguides.
AI.motivation: Efficient separation and localization of multifrequency acoustic waves are critical for underwater target recognition and acoustic energy harvesting. However, underwater topological rainbow trapping faces challenges due to complex fluid-solid interactions and the difficulty of combining long-range transport with frequency-selective localization in open systems.
AI.method: Two topological mechanisms are employed: (1) QVHE-based: a spatial gradient along a valley-Hall edge channel shifts local edge-state dispersion, causing different frequencies to localize at distinct positions. (2) QSHE-based: one-dimensional topological edge states couple to frequency-selective zero-dimensional higher-order corner states, enabling robust boundary transport followed by frequency-dependent transfer to remote corners. Both use SSAWs whose fields are confined near the structured surface and decay evanescently into surrounding water.
AI.result: Numerical simulations and experiments confirm frequency-dependent localization and persistence of transport pathways under structural defects. Both mechanisms achieve robust spectral and spatial demultiplexing (transport-then-confinement in the QSHE case), verified experimentally in open underwater SSAW platforms.
AI.conclusion: The proposed open SSAW platform enables robust physical-layer frequency demultiplexing, reducing reliance on digital signal processing. It offers significant potential for underwater target recognition and frequency-selective acoustic energy harvesting, successfully overcoming the open-system challenges previously limiting underwater topological rainbow trapping.

title: Memory with Onsager-Casimir symmetry: Rotating particle in a viscoelastic fluid
summary: We study the stochastic dynamics of a rotating Brownian particle in a non-Markovian fluid. Experimentally, we find that rotation enhances the long-time diffusivity of the particle and generates time-antisymmetric cross-correlations between orthogonal displacement components in the plane perpendicular to the rotation axis. To rationalize these observations, we introduce a minimal linear model in which a tracer is coupled to a slow bath degree of freedom and rotation enters through an advective coupling. Eliminating the bath variable yields a generalized Langevin equation with a non-reciprocal memory kernel. This kernel rotates in time, forming a logarithmic spiral, and it obeys Onsager-Casimir symmetry under reversal of the rotation vector, and the corresponding fluctuation-response relation. From the latter we obtain a geometric construction that links two-time cross-correlations to the transverse response of the particle in bulk. Unlike the ordinary Einstein relation, this relation involves the antisymmetric sector of the response. Our experiments and theory are in qualitative agreement, establishing rotating colloids in viscoelastic fluids as a minimal realization of Onsager-Casimir symmetry in time-nonlocal stochastic dynamics

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the stochastic dynamics of a rotating Brownian particle in a non-Markovian (viscoelastic) fluid. Experiments show rotation enhances long-time diffusivity and generates time-antisymmetric cross-correlations between orthogonal displacement components. A minimal linear model couples the tracer to a slow bath mode via advective rotation, yielding a generalized Langevin equation with a non-reciprocal memory kernel that rotates as a logarithmic spiral. The framework obeys Onsager-Casimir symmetry under rotation reversal and a generalized fluctuation-response relation linking two-time cross-correlations to the transverse response. Experiments and theory agree qualitatively, establishing rotating colloids in viscoelastic fluids as a minimal realization of Onsager-Casimir symmetry in time-nonlocal stochastic dynamics.
AI.motivation: To understand how rotation affects the transport properties of Brownian particles in non-Markovian (viscoelastic) fluids, and to establish a minimal theoretical framework that captures the coupling between rotation and memory, while demonstrating fundamental symmetries of time-nonlocal stochastic dynamics.
AI.method: Combines experiments on rotating Brownian particles in viscoelastic fluids with a minimal linear model where a tracer is coupled to a slow bath degree of freedom via an advective (rotation-induced) coupling. The bath variable is eliminated to obtain a generalized Langevin equation with a non-reciprocal, logarithmically rotating memory kernel. The framework is analyzed under Onsager-Casimir symmetry and a generalized fluctuation-response relation, yielding a geometric construction linking two-time cross-correlations to the transverse response.
AI.result: Rotation enhances long-time diffusivity and produces time-antisymmetric cross-correlations between orthogonal displacement components perpendicular to the rotation axis. The derived non-reciprocal memory kernel rotates in time as a logarithmic spiral and obeys Onsager-Casimir symmetry under reversal of the rotation vector. A generalized fluctuation-response relation connects two-time cross-correlations to the transverse response via the antisymmetric response sector. Experimental observations and theoretical predictions agree qualitatively.
AI.conclusion: Rotating colloids in viscoelastic fluids serve as a minimal experimental realization of Onsager-Casimir symmetry in time-nonlocal stochastic dynamics, demonstrating a clean and testable interplay between rotation, memory, and non-reciprocal response.

title: Magnetic circular dichroism of THz modes and selection rules of Raman-active optical phonons in the polar altermagnet candidate \ce{Mn2Mo3O8}
summary: We investigated the magnetic and vibrational excitations in the collinear altermagnet candidate \ce{Mn2Mo3O8} by temperature dependent Raman scattering and magneto-optical THz time-domain transmission spectroscopy. By comparison to \textit{ab initio} calculations accurately capturing the eigenfrequencies of the vibrational eigenmodes, we identify all optical phonons, including the lowest-lying Raman modes of $A_1$ and $E_2$ type, which had remained elusive in a previous Raman study. Moreover, we compare the selection rules for optically active phonons in the paramagnetic and the magnetically ordered phases of \ce{Mn2Mo3O8} and analyze the Raman selection rules with respect to pseudo-angular momentum conservation. No evidence of the expected splitting of the degenerate paramagnetic $E_2$ optical phonons into modes with circular polarization upon magnetic ordering could be resolved, likely due to weak spin-orbit coupling typical for Mn$^{2+}$. In contrast, we observe strong magnetic circular dichroism at a broad THz excitation band, emerging in the magnetically ordered state. This band, potentially originating from two-magnon excitations, is only electric-dipole active and features a field-dependent two-component fine structure. Its magnetic circular dichroism vanishes above the spin-flop transition at 4~T.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates magnetic and vibrational excitations in the collinear altermagnet candidate Mn2Mo3O8 using temperature-dependent Raman scattering and magneto-optical THz time-domain transmission spectroscopy, combined with ab initio calculations. All optical phonons including previously elusive lowest-lying A1 and E2 Raman modes were identified. No expected circular-polarization splitting of degenerate E2 phonons upon magnetic ordering was resolved (attributed to weak spin-orbit coupling in Mn2+), but strong magnetic circular dichroism was observed at a broad THz band potentially from two-magnon excitations, which vanishes above the spin-flop transition at 4 T.
AI.motivation: To fully characterize the phonon and magnetic excitation spectrum of the altermagnet candidate Mn2Mo3O8, identify previously missing low-energy Raman modes, test predicted phonon selection rules/pseudo-angular momentum effects under magnetic ordering, and explore magneto-optical phenomena in the THz range.
AI.method: Temperature-dependent Raman scattering and magneto-optical THz time-domain transmission spectroscopy, complemented by ab initio calculations of vibrational eigenmodes. Raman selection rules were analyzed in terms of pseudo-angular momentum conservation, and phonon behavior compared between paramagnetic and magnetically ordered phases.
AI.result: All optical phonons, including the previously elusive lowest-lying Raman modes of A1 and E2 type, were identified. No splitting of degenerate E2 phonons into circularly-polarized modes was observed upon magnetic ordering, likely due to weak spin-orbit coupling. Strong magnetic circular dichroism was observed at a broad THz band in the magnetically ordered state, potentially from two-magnon excitations, with a field-dependent two-component fine structure that vanishes above the spin-flop transition at 4 T.
AI.conclusion: The expected altermagnetic phonon splitting effects are absent or too weak to resolve in Mn2Mo3O8 due to weak spin-orbit coupling of Mn2+, while a strong electric-dipole-active THz band showing magnetic circular dichroism (likely two-magnon origin) is a prominent feature of the magnetically ordered state, disappearing above the spin-flop transition.

title: Correlated Insulator Moiré Bolometer
comment: 37 pages and 20 figures (main text and SI together)
summary: Light incident on an insulator is generally not expected to turn it into a metal without invoking intense ultrafast excitation that leads to transient structural transitions. Here we show that magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene tuned to half filling of the moiré band provides a notable exception to this expectation. We find that weak beam of long-wavelength photons, with energies comparable to the flat-band width, selectively heat the low-heat-capacity electronic subsystem, thereby suppressing the correlated gap. This produces a giant resistance change governed not by a persistent photocarrier population, but by the extreme sensitivity of a many-body correlated gap to weak electronic heating. The resulting photon-driven insulator-to-metal transition produces a broadband low-noise photoresponse with voltage responsivity exceeding millivolts per nW of absorbed power. The mechanism is dual to superconducting hot-electron response: radiation-heated electrons suppress a many-body order, but in reverse the correlated insulator melts into a metal, providing robustness to magnetic fields of several tesla and a sharp insulator-to-metal resistive contrast. Our results establish correlated flat-band systems as a platform for ultra-sensitive detection of faint long-wavelength radiation.

AI.tldr: Weak long-wavelength photons incident on magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene at half filling induce an insulator-to-metal transition by heating the electronic subsystem, suppressing the correlated gap through electron heating rather than persistent photocarriers, yielding a giant resistance change and ultra-sensitive photoresponse (mV/nW) robust to magnetic fields.
AI.motivation: Standard insulators require intense ultrafast excitation to become metallic, and the authors seek to find an exception where weak radiation can drive a correlated insulator into a metal, establishing a new platform for sensitive far-infrared/THz detection.
AI.method: Using magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene tuned to half filling of the moiré band, the authors illuminate the sample with weak long-wavelength photons whose energies match the flat-band width. The low-heat-capacity electronic subsystem is selectively heated, suppressing the correlated gap without structural changes or persistent photocarrier generation. The resistive response and voltage responsivity are measured under these conditions.
AI.result: A giant resistance change is observed governed by the extreme sensitivity of the correlated gap to electronic heating. The photon-driven insulator-to-metal transition yields broadband low-noise photoresponse with voltage responsivity exceeding millivolts per nW of absorbed power, and remains robust in magnetic fields of several tesla.
AI.conclusion: Correlated flat-band systems, and in particular magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene, establish a new platform for ultra-sensitive detection of faint long-wavelength radiation via a hot-electron-mediated correlated insulator-to-metal transition, which is dual to superconducting hot-electron bolometer physics.

title: Degradation of Proton Exchange Membrane Water Electrolyzers in Accelerated Stress Tests of Dynamic Load Cycling
summary: Proton exchange membrane water electrolysis (PEMWE) is a promising technology for harnessing intermittent renewable energy. This study experimentally investigates the degradation of PEMWE under fluctuating power supply, characterized by dynamic load cycling under accelerated stress test (AST). We focus on the effects of key parameters of dynamic loading, including the peak voltage and cycling frequency, in a set of simplified AST protocols designed to represent selected features of dynamic load fluctuations associated with variable renewable-energy operation. The results unveil the intricate relationship between the structural characteristics of the catalyst layer and the electrochemical performance. An elevated peak voltage accelerates the degradation in the initial phase of the AST. However, a low cycling frequency can mitigate the degradation by limiting the rise in various resistance forms, whereas a higher cycling frequency exacerbates the degradation primarily by increasing mass transport resistance, suggesting a frequency-sensitive deterioration of the system's components.

AI.tldr: This study experimentally investigates the degradation of proton exchange membrane water electrolysis (PEMWE) under fluctuating power supply using accelerated stress tests (AST) with dynamic load cycling. The key findings reveal that elevated peak voltage accelerates initial degradation, while low cycling frequency mitigates degradation by limiting resistance increases, and high cycling frequency exacerbates degradation primarily through increased mass transport resistance.
AI.motivation: PEMWE is a promising technology for harnessing intermittent renewable energy, but its degradation under fluctuating power supply conditions—which are inherent to renewable energy operation—is not well understood. This study aims to experimentally characterize how dynamic load parameters affect PEMWE degradation.
AI.method: Experimental investigation using accelerated stress tests (AST) with dynamic load cycling. The study systematically varies key loading parameters including peak voltage and cycling frequency in simplified AST protocols designed to represent features of variable renewable-energy operation, while monitoring degradation and resistance changes.
AI.result: Elevated peak voltage accelerates degradation in the initial phase of the AST. Low cycling frequency mitigates degradation by limiting the rise in various resistance forms, whereas higher cycling frequency exacerbates degradation primarily through increased mass transport resistance, revealing a frequency-sensitive deterioration of system components and an intricate relationship between catalyst layer structure and electrochemical performance.
AI.conclusion: The degradation of PEMWE under fluctuating power supply is strongly dependent on the parameters of dynamic loading—particularly peak voltage and cycling frequency. This frequency-sensitive and voltage-dependent degradation behavior provides important insights for designing more durable PEMWE systems and understanding their operational limits under real-world renewable energy conditions.

title: Griffiths phase in clique percolation in random geometric graphs
summary: In this study, we discuss the clique percolation in the ensembles of random geometric graphs with different kernels that quantify the geometrical constraints. For the sharp cut-off we find the wide Griffiths phase of extended criticality with the power-law behavior. One boundary of the Griffiths phase is the generalization of a percolation critical point for the ER ensemble when the percolation within the large but finite cluster emerges. The second boundary corresponds to the point in the parameter space when the percolation in the entire clustered system becomes available. For the power-law kernel, richer behavior with a clique-size-dependent boundary between the effective ER and geometric regimes has been identified. The Griffiths phase in this case exists as well. Finally, the pattern with the exponential kernel has been analyzed. We briefly discuss the possible applications of our findings.

AI.tldr: The paper studies clique percolation in random geometric graph ensembles with different kernel functions that encode geometric constraints. It identifies a wide Griffiths phase of extended criticality with power-law behavior for sharp cut-off kernels, generalizes the percolation critical point from the ER ensemble, and reveals richer clique-size-dependent behaviors for power-law and exponential kernels, with possible applications discussed.
AI.motivation: To understand how geometric constraints (represented by different kernel functions) affect clique percolation behavior in random geometric graphs, particularly the emergence and structure of Griffiths phases and transitions between ER-like and geometrically-dominated regimes.
AI.method: The study analyzes clique percolation in ensembles of random geometric graphs parametrized by different kernels that quantify geometric constraints. Three kernel types are examined: a sharp cut-off kernel, a power-law kernel, and an exponential kernel. The phase structure of each is characterized through analysis of percolation boundaries and cluster formation.
AI.result: For the sharp cut-off kernel, a wide Griffiths phase of extended criticality with power-law behavior is found, bounded by two distinct transitions: one generalizing the ER percolation critical point (percolation within large finite clusters), and another marking percolation in the entire clustered system. For the power-law kernel, a richer clique-size-dependent boundary between effective ER and geometric regimes is identified, with a Griffiths phase also present. The exponential kernel case is analyzed as well.
AI.conclusion: Geometric constraints introduced via different kernel functions significantly modify clique percolation behavior in random geometric graphs, producing Griffiths phases of extended criticality and regime-dependent boundaries. The findings have potential applications, which are briefly outlined.

title: Anisotropic transport of Josephson vortices in atomic-layer superconductors on vicinal surfaces
summary: Atomic steps have strong influences on surface two-dimensional superconductors. Josephson vortices formed at the atomic steps under magnetic fields may dominate transport phenomena at low temperatures, but its experimental verification is still lacking. Here, we report the vortex transport properties of atomic-layer superconductor Si(111)-$(\sqrt{7}\times\sqrt{3})$-In with vicinal surfaces, for which Josephson vortices are directly observed by scanning tunneling microscopy. A sharp drop in resistance with decreasing temperature $T$, detected under out-of-plane magnetic field $B$, reveals a distinctive anisotropy with respect to the atomic step direction. The anisotropy of sheet resistance, proportional to that of vortex mobility, amounts to the order of $10^3$ at intermediate magnetic fields. In the high-$T$ and low-$B$ region, Josephson vortices exhibit thermally excited creep motions with anisotropic activation energy $U_\mathrm{act}$. A further increase in $B$ suppresses $U_\mathrm{act}$ toward zero anisotropically, resulting in one-dimensional pinning-free vortex flow at $0.10 \lesssim B \lesssim 0.20$ T. At the lowest temperatures, the vortex motion is governed by quantum tunneling. A $B$-$T$ phase diagram constructed based on these measurements reveals multiple regions characterized by directionally dependent vortex-transport mechanisms.

AI.tldr: This paper reports direct STM observation of Josephson vortices at atomic steps in the atomic-layer superconductor Si(111)-(√7×√3)-In on vicinal surfaces, and characterizes their transport behaviors including anisotropic vortex mobility, thermally activated creep, one-dimensional pinning-free flow, and quantum tunneling, resulting in a B-T phase diagram of directionally dependent vortex-transport mechanisms.
AI.motivation: Atomic steps strongly influence surface two-dimensional superconductors, and Josephson vortices formed at these steps may dominate low-temperature transport. However, experimental verification of such vortex transport phenomena was previously lacking.
AI.method: The authors used scanning tunneling microscopy to directly observe Josephson vortices at atomic steps on vicinal Si(111)-(√7×√3)-In surfaces, combined with sheet resistance measurements under out-of-plane magnetic fields across a range of temperatures to probe vortex transport.
AI.result: A sharp resistance drop with decreasing temperature under out-of-plane magnetic field shows strong anisotropy relative to atomic step direction, with sheet resistance anisotropy (proportional to vortex mobility anisotropy) reaching ~10³ at intermediate fields. In high-T/low-B regimes, Josephson vortices exhibit thermally activated creep with anisotropic activation energy U_act. Increasing B suppresses U_act anisotropically to zero, yielding one-dimensional pinning-free vortex flow at 0.10-0.20 T. At lowest temperatures, vortex motion is governed by quantum tunneling.
AI.conclusion: A B-T phase diagram was constructed revealing multiple regions characterized by directionally dependent vortex-transport mechanisms, demonstrating that atomic-step-confined Josephson vortices dominate the transport properties of surface two-dimensional superconductors.

title: Gap distributions between successive personal bests in cricket: Data and Models
summary: Successive personal best performances provide a natural measure of progression in an athlete's career. Classical record theory predicts a universal gap distribution, $P(g)\sim 1/g$, for independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) sequences. However, sporting careers are shaped by learning, aging, changes in ability, and external influences that violate these assumptions. We investigate the statistics of inter-record gaps, defined as the number of innings between successive personal best scores, in cricket. Using career records of leading Test, ODI, and T20 players obtained from ESPN Cricinfo. We find that the empirical distributions are well described by truncated power law $P(g) \propto g^{-α} e^{-λg}$ with exponents in the range (0.799 $\leq α\leq$ 0.843). Much of this deviation disappears when the temporal ordering of innings is destroyed, indicating that career evolution plays a key role in shaping record occurrence. Bootstrap-shuffled careers, which preserve individual score distributions and career lengths while removing temporal ordering, yield significantly larger exponents ($α\approx 0.939\text{--}0.979$). These findings show that the progression of personal best performances retains information about the temporal organization of a player's career and cannot be fully explained by simple stochastic record processes. More generally, they illustrate how record statistics are altered in nonstationary and path-dependent systems.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes inter-record gaps (innings between successive personal best scores) across cricket careers in Test, ODI, and T20 formats using ESPN Cricinfo data. Empirical gap distributions follow truncated power laws with exponents α ≈ 0.799–0.843, deviating from i.i.d. record theory predictions (P(g)~1/g). Destroying temporal ordering via bootstrap shuffling raises exponents to α ≈ 0.939–0.979, showing career evolution (learning, aging, external factors) fundamentally shapes record occurrence in nonstationary systems.
AI.motivation: Classical record theory assumes i.i.d. sequences and predicts a universal gap distribution P(g)~1/g. However, real sporting careers violate these assumptions due to learning, aging, changing ability, and external influences. The authors aim to understand how record statistics are altered in nonstationary, path-dependent systems by studying personal best progression in cricket.
AI.method: The authors collect career records of leading Test, ODI, and T20 cricket players from ESPN Cricinfo. They compute inter-record gaps (innings between successive personal best scores) and fit empirical distributions to truncated power laws P(g) ∝ g^{-α} e^{-λg}. They compare with bootstrap-shuffled careers that preserve individual score distributions and career lengths but destroy temporal ordering to isolate the role of career evolution.
AI.result: Empirical inter-record gap distributions are well described by truncated power laws with exponents in range 0.799 ≤ α ≤ 0.843, deviating significantly from the i.i.d. prediction. Bootstrap-shuffled careers yield substantially larger exponents (α ≈ 0.939–0.979), much closer to the classical i.i.d. case, confirming that temporal ordering in careers is responsible for much of the observed deviation.
AI.conclusion: The progression of personal best performances retains information about the temporal organization of a player's career and cannot be fully explained by simple stochastic record processes. The findings broadly illustrate how record statistics are modified in nonstationary, path-dependent systems, with implications beyond sports to any system where performance evolves over time.

title: Active Passivation Tunes Hotspot Locations in GaN Transistors with In Situ Thermal Mechanical Visualization
summary: Efficient thermal dissipation has become critical in emerging electronic devices. However, most existing studies have primarily focused on engineering heat dissipation pathways, largely overlooking the intrinsic behavior of the heat source itself. We demonstrate an active passivation technology that proactively tunes hotspot locations in GaN transistors. By adjusting the active passivation layer length, the hotspot is shifted from the gate edge to the drain-side AP edge, establishing a clear one-to-one spatial correlation. In-situ thermal-mechanical visualization via micro-Raman thermography, combined with multi-physics electro-thermal-mechanical simulations, directly captures the spatial redistribution of both temperature and thermal stress profiles. Electrical analysis confirms that this hotspot migration is driven by the spatial shift of the peak electric field and localized Joule heating. This proactive heat-source tuning strategy provides critical design guidelines for power electronics.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates an active passivation technology for GaN transistors that proactively shifts hotspot locations from the gate edge to the drain-side active passivation edge by adjusting the passivation layer length. Using micro-Raman thermography and multi-physics simulations, the authors establish a spatial correlation between hotspot migration and the shift in peak electric field and localized Joule heating, offering design guidelines for power electronics thermal management.
AI.motivation: Existing thermal management studies focus on engineering heat dissipation pathways but largely overlook the intrinsic behavior of the heat source itself. This paper addresses the need to proactively control hotspot locations in power electronics by manipulating the heat source distribution rather than only improving heat removal.
AI.method: The authors employ active passivation with tunable layer length in GaN transistors. They use in-situ micro-Raman thermography for thermal-mechanical visualization and multi-physics electro-thermal-mechanical simulations to capture temperature and thermal stress redistribution. Electrical analysis links hotspot migration to spatial shifts in the peak electric field and localized Joule heating.
AI.result: Adjusting the active passivation layer length shifts the hotspot from the gate edge to the drain-side active passivation edge, establishing a clear one-to-one spatial correlation. The hotspot migration is shown to be driven by the spatial shift of the peak electric field and localized Joule heating, confirmed by both thermal and electrical analyses.
AI.conclusion: This proactive heat-source tuning strategy provides critical design guidelines for power electronics, representing a paradigm shift from passively managing heat dissipation to actively controlling heat generation location within devices.

title: Noise-enhanced temporal boundary states in non-Hermitian systems
summary: Time-periodic modulation introduces a synthetic degree of freedom to manipulate topological phases. This synthetic dimension can trigger a phase transition that localizes a boundary state at the temporal interface. Noise is widely deemed a fundamental threat to topological protection, universally anticipated to weaken or even destroy topological states. Here, we introduce periodically repeated temporal noise and fully random temporal noise into a 2D periodically driven non-Hermitian system. Paradoxically, under ensemble averaging, such temporal noise drives an exponential enhancement of the response intensity at the temporal interface. An averaged superoperator analysis shows that the noiseless band structure is preserved under both types of noise. Yet the noise increases the growth rate of growing modes while suppressing the decay rate of decaying ones. Finally, we experimentally realize the noise-enhanced temporal boundary state in a robotic metamaterial network. This finding establishes temporal noise as a constructive ingredient, enabling the unambiguous emergence of topological states and conferring exceptional robustness upon topological devices.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that temporal noise, contrary to conventional expectations, can exponentially enhance topological boundary states at temporal interfaces in a 2D periodically driven non-Hermitian system. Both periodically repeated and fully random temporal noise increase the growth rate of growing modes while suppressing decay rate of decaying modes, preserving the noiseless band structure. The phenomenon is verified experimentally in a robotic metamaterial network, establishing temporal noise as a constructive ingredient for topological devices.
AI.motivation: Time-periodic modulation creates synthetic dimensions for topological phase manipulation, at the cost of exposing systems to noise—which is conventionally believed to weaken or destroy topological states. The authors aim to challenge this assumption by investigating whether temporal noise can paradoxically enhance rather than degrade topological boundary states at temporal interfaces.
AI.method: The authors introduce two types of temporal noise (periodically repeated and fully random) into a 2D periodically driven non-Hermitian system. They employ an averaged superoperator analysis to examine the effective dynamics under ensemble averaging, comparing noise-free and noisy band structures and growth/decay rates of eigenmodes. They experimentally validate the findings using a robotic metamaterial network.
AI.result: Under ensemble averaging, both types of temporal noise drive an exponential enhancement of the response intensity at the temporal interface. The noiseless band structure is preserved under noise, yet the noise increases the growth rate of growing modes while suppressing the decay rate of decaying ones. The noise-enhanced temporal boundary state is experimentally realized in a robotic metamaterial network.
AI.conclusion: Temporal noise serves as a constructive ingredient rather than a destructive perturbation, enabling the unambiguous emergence of topological states and conferring exceptional robustness upon topological devices—inverting the conventional view that noise universally threatens topological protection.

title: Pressure-induced self-doping and Fermi surface reconstruction in UAs2
summary: Superconductivity has recently been reported in the heavy-fermion compound UAs2 under pressure, with the highest Tc among uranium-based correlated 5f-electron superconductors. To elucidate its microscopic origin, we investigate its electronic structure using density functional theory combined with dynamical mean-field theory (DFT+DMFT). At ambient pressure, our calculations reproduce the characteristic Kondo-lattice electronic structure, with flat hybridization bands near the Fermi energy around the Γ and M points, in good agreement with angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES). Under pressure, we find a systematic transfer of electrons from the more localized 5f5/2 orbitals to the more itinerant 5f7/2 orbitals, while the total U-5f occupancy remains nearly unchanged. This orbital-selective charge redistribution constitutes a pressure-induced self-doping effect that drives the 5f5/2 electrons from a localized Kondo regime toward a mixed-valence regime with enhanced charge fluctuations, leading to a dramatic reconstruction of the low-energy electronic structure. Remarkably, superconductivity emerges in the pressure range where the Fermi surface consists of two disconnected sheets with enhanced nesting, but disappears when they bend and merge into a corrugated three-dimensional cylinder. Our results provide an electronic-structure basis for understanding superconductivity in UAs2 and suggest that Fermi-surface nesting and charge fluctuations may contribute to the enhanced superconducting Tc, pointing to a possible distinction from conventional heavy-fermion superconductors.

AI.tldr: This paper uses DFT+DMFT calculations to study the electronic structure of the heavy-fermion superconductor UAs2 under pressure. It reveals that pressure induces an orbital-selective self-doping effect, transferring electrons from localized 5f5/2 to itinerant 5f7/2 orbitals, driving the system toward a mixed-valence regime with enhanced charge fluctuations. Superconductivity emerges when the Fermi surface consists of two disconnected sheets with strong nesting, and disappears when they merge into a corrugated 3D cylinder, suggesting Fermi-surface nesting and charge fluctuations contribute to the enhanced Tc.
AI.motivation: UAs2 exhibits the highest superconducting transition temperature among uranium-based correlated 5f-electron superconductors under pressure, but its microscopic mechanism remains unknown. The authors aim to elucidate the electronic-structure origin of this superconductivity.
AI.method: Density functional theory combined with dynamical mean-field theory (DFT+DMFT) is employed to compute the electronic structure of UAs2 at ambient pressure and under pressure, tracking orbital-resolved 5f occupancies, spectral functions, and Fermi-surface topology.
AI.result: The calculations reproduce the Kondo-lattice electronic structure at ambient pressure consistent with ARPES. Under pressure, an orbital-selective charge redistribution occurs (self-doping from 5f5/2 to 5f7/2), driving the system from a localized Kondo regime to a mixed-valence regime. Superconductivity emerges when the Fermi surface has two disconnected sheets with enhanced nesting but vanishes when they collapse into a corrugated cylindrical Fermi surface.
AI.conclusion: Fermi-surface nesting and pressure-induced charge fluctuations may be key ingredients enhancing Tc in UAs2, indicating a possible departure from conventional mechanisms of heavy-fermion superconductivity. The work provides an electronic-structure foundation for understanding superconductivity in this compound.

title: Spin selectivity induced by non-collinear spins in Rashba wires
summary: We report a previously overlooked general mechanism to obtain highly efficient spin selectivity in conventional time-reversal symmetric one-dimensional systems without invoking phase decoherence. We reveal that Rashba quantum wires featuring non-collinear spin states at the Fermi level inherently possess spin-selective transport properties. We show that this spin noncollinearity can be systematically designed and engineered by introducing an additional pseudospin degree of freedom - such as valley, sublattice, or orbital angular momentum - into spin-orbit coupled systems. By applying this framework to multi-subband semiconducting quantum wires and oxide nanowires, we establish a generalized route toward quantum-coherent spin selectivity up to 10 %. Our findings offer practical design principles for spin-selective transport devices.

AI.tldr: This paper reveals a previously overlooked general mechanism for achieving highly efficient spin selectivity in conventional time-reversal symmetric 1D systems without phase decoherence. The key insight is that Rashba quantum wires with non-collinear spin states at the Fermi level inherently exhibit spin-selective transport, and this noncollinearity can be engineered by introducing additional pseudospin degrees of freedom (valley, sublattice, or orbital angular momentum). Applied to multi-subband semiconductor quantum wires and oxide nanowires, the framework yields quantum-coherent spin selectivity up to 10%, providing practical design principles for spin-selective transport devices.
AI.motivation: To overcome limitations in spin-selective transport that typically require phase decoherence or broken time-reversal symmetry, the authors seek a general, overlooked mechanism for achieving highly efficient spin selectivity in conventional time-reversal symmetric 1D systems.
AI.method: The authors propose that non-collinear spin states at the Fermi level in Rashba quantum wires provide inherent spin selectivity. They show that this noncollinearity can be systematically engineered by introducing an additional pseudospin degree of freedom (valley, sublattice, or orbital angular momentum) into spin-orbit coupled systems, and apply this framework to multi-subband semiconductor quantum wires and oxide nanowires.
AI.result: The framework establishes a generalized route toward quantum-coherent spin selectivity reaching up to 10% in multi-subband semiconductor quantum wires and oxide nanowires, without requiring phase decoherence.
AI.conclusion: The findings provide practical design principles for spin-selective transport devices, expanding the toolkit for spintronic applications in conventional time-reversal symmetric systems.

title: Committors and Reaction Rates from Trial Functions That Violate the Boundary Conditions
summary: The committor is the optimal reaction coordinate for a rare transition: it pinpoints the transition state and fixes the rate, and it governs events from protein folding to crystal nucleation. It minimises a Dirichlet energy, whose value at the minimum is the reactive flux, over functions that vanish on the reactant state and equal one on the product state. In high dimensions such a trial space is very hard to build. Here we rewrite the variational principle so that the boundary conditions are replaced by a normalisation of one boundary observable, the fidelity. Any trial function is then admissible, including functions that cannot satisfy the boundary values at all. On this basis we estimate the high-dimensional committor and rates from one-dimensional profiles along projected coordinates, taking as input only pre-existing equilibrium or reweighted configurations, a diffusion constant estimate, and the two state definitions. The optimum has a closed form that is cheap to evaluate. We obtain committors for AIB9 and villin HP-35 in full torsion space, and folding and unfolding rates for chignolin from umbrella sampling alone.

AI.tldr: This paper reformulates the variational principle for the committor—the optimal reaction coordinate for rare transitions—by replacing boundary conditions with a normalization constraint on a boundary observable (the fidelity). This makes any trial function admissible, allowing estimation of high-dimensional committors and rates from one-dimensional projected profiles using only pre-existing equilibrium configurations, a diffusion constant estimate, and state definitions. The optimal solution has a closed, cheap-to-evaluate form, demonstrated on AIB9, villin HP-35, and chignolin folding.
AI.motivation: The committor is the optimal reaction coordinate for rare transitions, but building a trial function space in high dimensions is extremely difficult because it requires functions satisfying specific boundary values on reactant and product states.
AI.method: The authors rewrite the committor variational principle so that boundary conditions are replaced by a normalization of one boundary observable, the fidelity. This makes any trial function admissible. They estimate the high-dimensional committor and rates from one-dimensional profiles along projected coordinates, using only equilibrium or reweighted configurations, a diffusion constant estimate, and state definitions. The optimum has a closed form that is cheap to evaluate.
AI.result: The method produces committors for AIB9 and villin HP-35 in full torsion space, and folding and unfolding rates for chignolin from umbrella sampling alone, demonstrating applicability to real protein systems.
AI.conclusion: By removing the boundary-condition constraint and replacing it with a fidelity normalization, the variational principle becomes tractable in high dimensions, enabling committor and rate estimation from readily available equilibrium data.

title: Tunneling the Loss Landscape: Bypassing Memorization with Monte Carlo Parameter Swapping
summary: Grokking is a striking phenomenon in neural network training, where a model can undergo a prolonged period of pure memorization before abrupt generalization.
