The method is based on the backbone curve obtained from ringdown measurements, making it inherently resilient to small frequency fluctuations while explicitly accounting for both symmetry-breaking and non-symmetry-breaking nonlinearities. To validate the approach, we perform complementary ringdown and frequency-response measurements on the nanostring resonator and benchmark the backbone-based extraction against established frequency-response techniques. The comparison confirms the accuracy of the proposed framework and demonstrates its advantages over conventional methods for nonlinear characterization.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a robust framework for extracting conservative nonlinearities from high-Q nanomechanical string resonators using backbone curves obtained from ringdown measurements, validated against conventional frequency-response techniques.
AI.motivation: Nanomechanical resonators offer high sensitivity for studying nonlinear dynamics, but accurately extracting conservative nonlinearities remains challenging, especially in the presence of small frequency fluctuations and various types of nonlinearities.
AI.method: The authors use ringdown measurements to construct the backbone curve, which serves as the basis for extracting conservative nonlinearities. This approach inherently tolerates small frequency fluctuations and accounts for both symmetry-breaking and non-symmetry-breaking nonlinearities. Complementary ringdown and frequency-response measurements were performed on a nanostring resonator, and the backbone-based extraction was benchmarked against established frequency-response techniques.
AI.result: The comparison between backbone-based extraction and conventional frequency-response techniques confirms the accuracy of the proposed framework and demonstrates its advantages for nonlinear characterization of nanomechanical resonators.
AI.conclusion: The backbone-curve-based framework provides a more robust and accurate alternative to conventional frequency-response methods for extracting conservative nonlinearities in nanomechanical string resonators, particularly beyond the Duffing regime.

title: Composite quantum geometry of superconductors
summary: The interplay of superconductivity and the quantum geometry of the normal state has recently been the subject of an array of studies, especially regarding the superfluid weight. In this work, we turn our attention to the quantum geometry of the superconducting state itself, set by the Bogoliubov-de Gennes (BdG) Hamiltonian, which dictates the geometric and topological properties of superconductivity. We show that under three general conditions, namely superconducting fitness, orbital uniformity of the superconducting pairing, and absence of normal-state spin-flip terms, the BdG quantum geometry exactly separates into a sum of the normal-state quantum geometry and an additional pairing quantum geometry, thereby displaying a simple composite structure. We show that this separation holds for all spin-singlet and -triplet pairings, including nonunitary spin-triplet pairing. We further provide explicit analytical formulas for the pairing quantum geometry for all these cases. These results establish how superconducting pairing alone easily drives both topology and a finite quantum metric, thus being present even in topological trivial or flat band superconductors, with no normal state quantum geometry. To complement these results, we also derive the BdG quantum geometry of a general two-orbital spin-singlet superconductor with non-uniform pairing and finite superconducting fitness. Here, our explicit analytical results establish a non-separable composite BdG quantum geometry, with the normal state and pairing contributions generally intertwining, thereby producing even more possibilities for finite quantum geometry. Our results provide design rules for creating superconductors and superconducting hybrid structures with nontrivial topology and finite quantum metric and will additionally help in the experimental diagnosis of unconventional superconductivity.

AI.tldr: This work shows that under three general conditions (superconducting fitness, orbital uniformity of pairing, and absence of normal-state spin-flip terms), the BdG quantum geometry of a superconductor exactly separates into normal-state quantum geometry plus an independent pairing quantum geometry, valid for all spin-singlet and -triplet pairings including nonunitary cases. Explicit analytical formulas are provided, demonstrating that pairing alone can drive topology and finite quantum metric even in topologically trivial or flat-band superconductors. For a general two-orbital spin-singlet superconductor with non-uniform pairing, a non-separable intertwined BdG quantum geometry is derived instead. These results provide design rules for unconventional superconductivity with nontrivial topology and quantum metric.
AI.motivation: While prior work focused on how normal-state quantum geometry affects superconducting properties like superfluid weight, this paper shifts attention to the quantum geometry of the superconducting state itself—set by the BdG Hamiltonian—which dictates the geometric and topological properties of superconductivity, and seeks a systematic understanding of how pairing alone contributes to quantum geometry and topology.
AI.method: The authors derive exact separability conditions for BdG quantum geometry into normal-state and pairing contributions under three general conditions: superconducting fitness, orbital uniformity of pairing, and absence of normal-state spin-flip terms. They provide explicit analytical formulas for pairing quantum geometry covering all spin-singlet/triplet pairings (including nonunitary spin-triplet). They further analyze a general two-orbital spin-singlet superconductor with non-uniform pairing and finite fitness to reveal the non-separable, intertwined composite geometry.
AI.result: The BdG quantum geometry exactly decomposes into normal-state plus pairing contributions when the three conditions hold, valid for all pairing classes. Pairing alone can drive both nontrivial topology and finite quantum metric even in topologically trivial or flat-band systems with no normal-state quantum geometry. For non-uniform two-orbital cases, the composite geometry is non-separable, with normal and pairing contributions intertwining and generating further possibilities.
AI.conclusion: The results establish clear design rules for creating superconductors and hybrid superconducting structures with nontrivial topology and finite quantum metric, and provide analytical tools that will aid in the experimental diagnosis of unconventional superconductivity.

title: Spin- and Angle-resolved Photoelectron Spectroscopy Study of the Quantum Spin Hall Insulator Bismuthene and its Precursor Phase
summary: Recent studies have revealed that a confined bismuth layer at the graphene/SiC interface can be reversibly switched between a topologically trivial precursor phase and the quantum spin Hall insulator bismuthene. Here, we present a detailed spin- and angle-resolved photoelectron spectroscopy study of both structures, resolving the spin texture of their low-energy electronic states. Owing to the strong intrinsic spin-orbit coupling of bismuth and the asymmetric confinement potential at the interface, the valence bands of both structures are Rashba-split. We demonstrate the expected spin-momentum locking for both phases and Kramers' doublets through the investigation of the valence bands' spin polarization at multiple positions in reciprocal space.

AI.tldr: A spin- and angle-resolved photoelectron spectroscopy study resolving the spin texture of the topologically trivial precursor phase and quantum spin Hall insulator bismuthene at the graphene/SiC interface, demonstrating Rashba-split valence bands with spin-momentum locking and Kramers' doublets in both phases.
AI.motivation: To provide a detailed experimental characterization of the spin texture of both the topologically trivial precursor phase and the quantum spin Hall bismuthene, since understanding the spin-resolved electronic structure is essential for confirming the topological nature and spin-momentum locking in these systems.
AI.method: Spin- and angle-resolved photoelectron spectroscopy (spin-ARPES) performed on both bismuth layer structures at the graphene/SiC interface, with spin polarization measurements of the valence bands' low-energy electronic states at multiple positions in reciprocal space.
AI.result: Both structures exhibit Rashba-split valence bands due to strong intrinsic spin-orbit coupling of bismuth and the asymmetric confinement potential at the interface. The expected spin-momentum locking for both phases and Kramers' doublets were demonstrated through spin polarization analysis.
AI.conclusion: The study experimentally confirms the spin-momentum locking and Kramers' doublet nature of the low-energy electronic states in both the trivial precursor and bismuthene phases, providing direct spectroscopic evidence for the topological characteristics of these confined bismuth layers.

title: Emission dynamics in zincblende InAsxP1-x quantum dots in InP nanowires: influence of quantum dot size, composition and nanowire geometry
comment: 22 pages, 7 figures, submitted to: Photonics and Nanostructures - Fundamentals and Applications
summary: Hereby, we present an experimental and theoretical investigation of emission dynamics in zincblende InAsxP1-x quantum dots (QDs) embedded in InP nanowires (NWs) grown via vapour-liquid-solid mechanism by chemical beam epitaxy, using Au nanoparticles as a nucleation catalyst. By measuring time-resolved photoluminescence from an ensemble of QD-NWs it was possible to determine the exciton lifetime dependence on QD composition and height. Changes in the InP shell thickness surrounding the InP NW stem with a QD, brought additional insight into the influence of photonic environment on the carrier dynamics. High-resolution transmission electron microscopy, combined with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy, provided actual structural parameters. The experimentally obtained lifetimes were interpreted in the light of results of 8 band kp calculations combined with configuration-interaction model to take into account the Coulomb interactions and finite-difference time domain photonic simulations to include the effect of optical confinement. The full understanding of the experimental results required considering both, the changes in the QD potential and the Purcell effect, the latter leading to spontaneous emission inhibition in the case of NWs with thin InP shell.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an experimental and theoretical study of emission dynamics in zincblende InAsxP1-x quantum dots embedded in InP nanowires grown by chemical beam epitaxy. Time-resolved photoluminescence measurements determine exciton lifetime dependence on QD composition and height, and shell thickness effects on carrier dynamics. Experimental lifetimes are interpreted using 8-band kp calculations with configuration-interaction model and FDTD photonic simulations, revealing that both QD potential changes and the Purcell effect (leading to spontaneous emission inhibition for thin shells) explain the results.
AI.motivation: To understand the emission dynamics and exciton lifetimes in InAsxP1-x quantum dots embedded in InP nanowires, clarifying the roles of QD composition, height, and photonic environment (shell thickness) on carrier recombination dynamics.
AI.method: Vapour-liquid-solid chemical beam epitaxy growth with Au nanoparticle catalysts; time-resolved photoluminescence on QD-NW ensembles; high-resolution transmission electron microscopy and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy for structural parameters; 8-band kp calculations combined with configuration-interaction model for Coulomb interactions; finite-difference time-domain photonic simulations for optical confinement effects.
AI.result: Exciton lifetime depends on QD composition and height; shell thickness influences carrier dynamics via photonic environment. The full understanding required accounting for both QD potential changes and the Purcell effect, with spontaneous emission inhibition observed in NWs with thin InP shells.
AI.conclusion: Both intrinsic QD properties (potential, composition, height) and extrinsic photonic effects (Purcell effect via shell thickness) govern emission dynamics in these QD-NW systems, with thin shells leading to spontaneous emission inhibition.

title: Superconducting dome due to the Fano-Feshbach shape resonance in artificial high-Tc superlattices
summary: In this work we provide compelling experimental validation of the Bianconi Perali Valletta (BPV) theory predicting a superconducting dome based on a quantum material design of Artificial High TC Superlattices (AHTS) made with a selected nanoscale heterostructure geometry. These AHTS are SNSN superlattices of quantum wells of period d, composed of first units, superconducting doped Mott insulator layers with Rashba spin orbit coupling (S) of thickness L, intercalated by second units, normal metal spacers (N). In these superlattices, grown by molecular beam epitaxy (MBE), the experimental superconducting dome is obtained by material quantum design changing the chemical potential via the quantum geometrical factor L/d which tunes the Fano-Feshbach shape resonance in the pair transfer between superconducting gaps in the BCS regime and different gaps in the BEC-BCS crossover. Here we present a systematic magneto-transport study of AHTS artificial superlattices across the full doping range of the superconducting dome, from the deeply underdoped to the overdoped regime, using pulsed magnetic fields up to 72 T. By varying the L/d ratio, we tune the effective hole concentration delta=0.45(1-L/d) and map the evolution of the resistive transitions, the upper critical magnetic field and the Ginzburg-Landau coherence length

AI.tldr: This paper presents systematic experimental validation of the Bianconi-Perali-Valletta (BPV) theory for a superconducting dome in Artificial High-TC Superlattices (AHTS) — SNSN superlattices of quantum wells combining superconducting doped Mott insulator layers (with Rashba spin-orbit coupling) and normal metal spacers. By tuning the quantum geometrical factor L/d (thickness ratio), the authors control the effective hole concentration and map the full superconducting dome from underdoped to overdoped regimes using pulsed magnetic fields up to 72 T, tracking resistive transitions, upper critical fields, and Ginzburg-Landau coherence lengths.
AI.motivation: To provide compelling experimental evidence for the BPV theory, which predicts a superconducting dome in artificially designed high-temperature superconducting superlattices via Fano-Feshbach shape resonances in pair transfer between BCS and BEC-BCS crossover gaps, tuned by quantum material design.
AI.method: AHTS SNSN superlattices (superconducting doped Mott insulator with Rashba SOC layers of thickness L, intercalated with normal metal spacers) are grown by molecular beam epitaxy. The quantum geometrical factor L/d tunes the chemical potential and hole concentration (delta=0.45(1-L/d)). Systematic magneto-transport measurements are performed in pulsed magnetic fields up to 72 T across the entire superconducting dome doping range.
AI.result: The experimental superconducting dome is obtained across the full doping range, from deeply underdoped to overdoped regimes. By varying L/d, the evolution of resistive transitions, upper critical magnetic field, and Ginzburg-Landau coherence length is mapped.
AI.conclusion: The results provide compelling experimental validation of the BPV theory for superconducting domes in artificial high-TC superlattices, demonstrating that quantum design via the geometrical factor L/d can control superconductivity through Fano-Feshbach shape resonances.

title: Resolving High-Energy States of Interlayer Excitons in MoSe$_2$/WSe$_2$ Heterostructures
summary: High-energy states of interlayer excitons (IXs) in van der Waals heterostructures remain largely unexplored despite their importance for understanding many-body interactions and nonlinear optical phenomena. Here, we use photoluminescence excitation (PLE) spectroscopy to resolve a Rydberg-like series of excited IX states in MoSe$_2$/WSe$_2$ heterostructures. We observe multiple PLE resonances below the intralayer exciton energies, which we assign to the 2s-, 3s-, and 4s-like states of the IXs. These resonances are consistently observed across heterostructures with different twist angles, indicating that the high-energy state spectrum is only weakly affected by the twist angle. Wannier-exciton calculations incorporating screened Coulomb interactions reproduce the overall energy scale and qualitative trends of the measured Rydberg-like series, supporting the assignment of the observed resonances. Our findings demonstrate that PLE provides direct experimental access to the previously unexplored high-energy IX states in van der Waals heterostructures.

AI.tldr: The paper uses photoluminescence excitation (PLE) spectroscopy to resolve a Rydberg-like series of excited interlayer exciton (IX) states (2s, 3s, 4s) in MoSe2/WSe2 heterostructures, supported by Wannier-exciton calculations that reproduce the energy scale and trends. The high-energy IX states are found to be only weakly affected by twist angle.
AI.motivation: High-energy states of interlayer excitons (IXs) in van der Waals heterostructures remain largely unexplored, despite being important for understanding many-body interactions and nonlinear optical phenomena.
AI.method: Photoluminescence excitation (PLE) spectroscopy is used to probe excited IX states in MoSe2/WSe2 heterostructures. Comparisons are made across heterostructures with different twist angles, and Wannier-exciton calculations incorporating screened Coulomb interactions are performed to interpret the observed resonances.
AI.result: Multiple PLE resonances below the intralayer exciton energies are observed, assigned to 2s-, 3s-, and 4s-like states of IXs. These resonances are consistently observed across different twist angles, and Wannier-exciton calculations reproduce the overall energy scale and qualitative trends of the Rydberg-like series.
AI.conclusion: PLE provides direct experimental access to previously unexplored high-energy IX states in van der Waals heterostructures, enabling further studies of many-body interactions and nonlinear optical phenomena in these systems.

title: Ultrahigh Intrinsic Hole Mobilities in $M$N$_2$ ($M$= Mo and W) at Room Temperature
summary: High-mobility $p$-type semiconductors are essential for advanced electronic devices but remain scarce. Here, using a hierarchical screening framework that combines first-principles calculations with Boltzmann transport theory, we identify $M$N$_2$ ($M$= Mo and W) family as polar semiconductors with exceptionally high intrinsic hole mobilities. In particular, 1H-WN$_2$ exhibits a room-temperature hole mobility exceeding $10^{4}$~$\mathrm{cm^2\,V^{-1}\,s^{-1}}$. This exceptional transport performance arises from the synergistic suppression of polar-optical-phonon and acoustic-phonon scattering, together with a reduced intervalley-scattering phase space induced by spin--valley locking. These effects arise from anomalously small Born effective charges, strong covalent N--N bonds, and orbital hybridization between N-$2p_x$/$2p_y$ and W-$5d_{xy}$/$5d_{x^2-y^2}$ in the N$_2$-dimer-based structure. Our results establish MoN$_2$ and WN$_2$ as a promising class of high-mobility polar semiconductors and introduce a crystal-structure-based strategy for concurrently suppressing multiple electron--phonon scattering channels, thereby revising design principles for high-mobility materials.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies MN₂ (M=Mo, W) family as polar semiconductors with exceptionally high intrinsic hole mobilities via hierarchical first-principles screening. 1H-WN₂ shows room-temperature hole mobility exceeding 10⁴ cm²V⁻¹s⁻¹, attributed to suppressed polar-optical-phonon and acoustic-phonon scattering, plus reduced intervalley scattering from spin-valley locking.
AI.motivation: High-mobility p-type semiconductors are crucial for advanced electronics but are rare, creating a need to discover new materials with exceptional hole transport properties.
AI.method: A hierarchical screening framework combining first-principles calculations with Boltzmann transport theory was employed to systematically evaluate hole mobilities in MN₂ (M=Mo, W) compounds.
AI.result: 1H-WN₂ exhibits a room-temperature hole mobility exceeding 10⁴ cm²V⁻¹s⁻¹, resulting from synergistic suppression of polar-optical-phonon and acoustic-phonon scattering and reduced intervalley-scattering phase space from spin-valley locking.
AI.conclusion: MoN₂ and WN₂ are established as a promising class of high-mobility polar semiconductors. The work introduces a crystal-structure-based strategy for concurrently suppressing multiple electron-phonon scattering channels, revising design principles for high-mobility materials.

title: Complete Structural Determination of Mesostructural Dodecagonal Quasicrystalline Particles
summary: Quasicrystals have revolutionized our understanding of order in solids by demonstrating exotic structural and physicochemical properties with diverse potential applications. Despite the development of various theoretical models and experimental techniques to describe quasicrystal structures, the precise determination of local three dimensional (3D) arrangements of constituent atoms, or of secondary building units such as clusters or micelles, remains elusive. This challenge is particularly acute in self assembled soft matter quasicrystalline systems, where the complex assembly of molecular groups introduces additional defects and structural modulations. Herein, we report the first complete structural determination of self-assembled mesostructural dodecagonal quasicrystalline particles. Employing advanced electron tomography, combined with dedicated structural tracing and processing workflows, the 3D coordinates of all nodal sites were extracted. This approach reveals that the actual structure deviates from the conventionally assumed tetrahedral close packing geometry, exhibiting diverse coordination environments and displacive fluctuations. We identified and quantified rotational intergrowths arising from node exchange, as well as various defects and disorder, with these features discernible only through 3D analysis. Additionally, we propose a simplified two-layer stacking of isomorphic hexagonal model to form dodecagonal quasicrystal. This work advances our understanding of soft-matter dodecagonal quasicrystals and paves the way for detailed structural elucidation of self-assembled systems.

AI.tldr: The paper reports the first complete 3D structural determination of self-assembled dodecagonal quasicrystalline particles using advanced electron tomography, revealing deviations from the assumed tetrahedral close packing geometry, diverse coordination environments, displacive fluctuations, rotational intergrowths, and defects. A simplified two-layer stacking model of isomorphic hexagons is proposed to form the dodecagonal quasicrystal.
AI.motivation: Precise determination of local 3D atomic arrangements in quasicrystals remains elusive, particularly in self-assembled soft matter quasicrystalline systems where molecular assembly introduces defects and structural modulations. There is a need for a complete structural determination to resolve the actual geometry versus conventional assumptions.
AI.method: Advanced electron tomography combined with dedicated structural tracing and processing workflows was used to extract 3D coordinates of all nodal sites in self-assembled mesostructural dodecagonal quasicrystalline particles.
AI.result: The actual structure deviates from conventionally assumed tetrahedral close packing, exhibiting diverse coordination environments and displacive fluctuations. Rotational intergrowths from node exchange, along with various defects and disorder, were identified and quantified—features only discernible via 3D analysis. A simplified two-layer isomorphic hexagonal stacking model was proposed for the dodecagonal quasicrystal.
AI.conclusion: This work advances the understanding of soft-matter dodecagonal quasicrystals and establishes a pathway for detailed structural elucidation of self-assembled systems.

title: Atomic-scale reactivity of the CeO$_2$~(100) surface reconstructions by scanning probe microscopy
summary: The atomic-scale structure and reactivity of the CeO$_2$(100) surface remain poorly understood because its intrinsic polarity and low stability lead to complex reconstructions. Here, we combine scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) and atomic force microscopy (AFM) experiments using oxygen-terminated probes with first-principles modeling to investigateCeO$_2$(100) films at the atomic scale. STM revealsthe patterns associated with the CeO$_4$-pyramid-terminated (2$\times$2) and oxygen-terminated c(2$\times$2) reconstructions, the latter forming small patches at step edges. AFM imaging andforce spectroscopy provide direct identification of the exposed surface atomic species and revealfeatures compatible with adsorbate-related perturbations. Density functional theoryand AFM simulations reproduce the main experimental observations and show that the interaction with the probe isgoverned by the short-range Pauli repulsion for the oxygen-terminated surface, while that for the CeO$_4$-terminated surface is markedly affected by electrostatic contributions, highlighting the limits of simple probe models for describing copper-oxide probes on strongly corrugated polar oxide surfaces. For CeO$_4$-terminated surfaces, STM alone is not a robust fingerprint of the local reduction state, as STM simulations of the oxidized and reduced surfaces yield a similar apparent contrast due to the interplay between the vacuum decay of the local density of states and the highly corrugated surface geometry. In contrast, for the oxygen-terminated reconstruction, STM is sensitive to the reduced state and provides information on the distribution of Ce$^{3+}$ and Ce$^{4+}$ ions in the first Ce layer. These results establish an experimental-theoretical framework that connects surface reconstruction, atomic-site assignment, local force response, and adsorbate sensitivity on complex oxide surfaces.

AI.tldr: This study combines STM and AFM experiments with first-principles modeling to characterize the atomic-scale structure and reactivity of the polar CeO2(100) surface, identifying two reconstructions (CeO4-pyramid-terminated (2×2) and oxygen-terminated c(2×2)), and revealing how probe-surface interactions differ between them. It also shows that STM alone is an unreliable fingerprint of local reduction state on CeO4-terminated surfaces, while it is sensitive to Ce3+/Ce4+ distribution on oxygen-terminated surfaces.
AI.motivation: The atomic-scale structure and reactivity of the CeO2(100) surface are poorly understood due to its intrinsic polarity and low stability, which lead to complex reconstructions that have not been thoroughly investigated at the atomic level.
AI.method: The authors combine scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) and atomic force microscopy (AFM) with oxygen-terminated probes, alongside first-principles calculations including density functional theory and AFM/STM simulations.
AI.result: Two reconstructions were resolved: a CeO4-pyramid-terminated (2×2) and an oxygen-terminated c(2×2) reconstruction. AFM identified exposed surface atomic species and showed the probe interaction is governed by short-range Pauli repulsion on oxygen-terminated surfaces but is markedly affected by electrostatic contributions on CeO4-terminated surfaces. STM contrast is not a robust fingerprint of local reduction state on CeO4-terminated surfaces, but is sensitive to Ce3+/Ce4+ distribution on oxygen-terminated surfaces.
AI.conclusion: The results establish an experimental-theoretical framework connecting surface reconstruction, atomic-site assignment, local force response, and adsorbate sensitivity on complex oxide surfaces, while also highlighting limitations of simple probe models on strongly corrugated polar oxide surfaces.

title: Time reversal symmetry broken quantum spin hall effect in pseudospin-1 Dirac-Rashba system
summary: The Quantum spin Hall (QSH) phase is conventionally understood to be protected by time-reversal symmetry (TRS). Here, we theoretically investigated the fate of the QSH phase in a pseudospin-1 fermionic $α-\mathcal{T}_3$ system in the presence of a TRS-breaking ferromagnetic exchange field and spin-nonconserving Rashba spin-orbit coupling. Despite broken TRS, the QSH phase survives over a finite parameter regime and is characterised by a non-zero projected spin-Chern number $C_σ(σ= \uparrow, \downarrow)$, protected by a spin-spectral gap. In the absence of Rashba coupling, the QSH phase remains robust up to an $α$-dependent critical exchange field. Rashba SOC qualitatively reshapes the phase diagram by driving transitions into two distinct quantum anomalous Hall (QAH) phases: a $C=2$ phase, irrespective of $α$-values, and a $C=1$ phase for $α\neq 0,1$, which is further identified as a valley-polarized QAH phase arising from a single valley. Rotating the magnetization to in-plane gaps out the first-order helical edge states and gives rise to second-order topological insulator (SOTI) phases that host localized corner states in suitable finite geometry. We further identify a topological phase transition between two different SOTI phases, mediated by nanoribbon edge states at an exchange field equal to $α$. These results establish spin-resolved topology in a higher pseudospin system as well as the $α-\mathcal{T}_3$ lattice as a versatile platform for engineering and controlling multiple topological phases through magnetic exchange and spin-orbit coupling.

AI.tldr: The paper theoretically investigates the quantum spin Hall (QSH) phase in a pseudospin-1 fermionic α-𝒯₃ system with broken time-reversal symmetry (TRS) due to a ferromagnetic exchange field and Rashba spin-orbit coupling. Despite broken TRS, the QSH phase survives over a finite parameter regime characterized by a non-zero spin-Chern number, and the system exhibits rich phase transitions into distinct quantum anomalous Hall (QAH) and second-order topological insulator (SOTI) phases, establishing the α-𝒯₃ lattice as a versatile platform for engineering multiple topological phases.
AI.motivation: Conventionally, the QSH phase is believed to be protected by time-reversal symmetry. This work challenges and extends this paradigm by exploring whether the QSH phase can survive in a higher pseudospin (pseudospin-1) α-𝒯₃ system even when TRS is broken by magnetic exchange and Rashba spin-orbit coupling, thereby uncovering new topological phases and enriching the understanding of spin-resolved topology.
AI.method: The authors theoretically model a pseudospin-1 fermionic α-𝒯₃ lattice with a TRS-breaking ferromagnetic exchange field and spin-nonconserving Rashba spin-orbit coupling. They compute the projected spin-Chern number C_σ, analyze the spin-spectral gap, map out phase diagrams as a function of exchange field and α, examine magnetization rotation to in-plane to study first-order helical edge states, and identify SOTI phases with corner states in finite geometries, including a topological phase transition mediated by nanoribbon edge states.
AI.result: The QSH phase survives despite broken TRS over a finite parameter regime, characterized by a non-zero projected spin-Chern number and protected by a spin-spectral gap. Without Rashba coupling, the QSH phase is robust up to an α-dependent critical exchange field. Rashba SOC drives transitions into two distinct QAH phases: a C=2 phase for all α-values and a C=1 valley-polarized QAH phase for α≠0,1. Rotating magnetization to in-plane gaps out first-order helical edge states and gives rise to SOTI phases hosting localized corner states, including a topological phase transition between two SOTI phases at an exchange field equal to α.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes spin-resolved topology in a higher pseudospin system, demonstrating that QSH topology can persist without TRS, and positions the α-𝒯₃ lattice as a versatile platform for engineering and controlling multiple topological phases (QSH, QAH, and SOTI) through magnetic exchange and spin-orbit coupling.

title: Conditional grain-graph diffusion for property-guided inverse design of polycrystalline microstructures
summary: Graph representations compactly encode polycrystalline microstructures while retaining grain topology and grain boundary information. We present a conditional graph diffusion framework for property-guided inverse design of dual-phase Ti-6Al-4V microstructures. An enhanced grain graph neural network (GNN) with grain boundary edge features, learnable node and edge embeddings, and multi-statistic pooling serves as a forward surrogate for stress prediction and candidate evaluation. The conditional diffusion model generates candidates through reverse diffusion under prescribed α-phase volume fraction, elastic modulus, and yield-stress proxy targets. Across four target regimes and independently seeded starting sets, generated candidates consistently approach the prescribed properties, including a target outside the property envelope of the existing microstructures. Local crystallographic consistency is evaluated post-generation from deviations from the Burgers orientation relationship (BOR). BOR-aware ranking increases mean BOR consistency by up to 44.9% and 56.4% for the in- and out-of-envelope targets, respectively, while maintaining property alignment. Finite element validation of the five best candidates in each primary design case yields a maximum absolute relative error of 1.0% in their mean properties. In a representative benchmark, diffusion requires 32 candidate evaluations per input graph, compared with approximately 40,000 for random search and evolutionary optimization, and reduces runtime by approximately two orders of magnitude in the tested implementations. These results establish conditional grain-graph diffusion as an efficient framework for property-guided polycrystalline microstructure design.

AI.tldr: A conditional graph diffusion framework for property-guided inverse design of dual-phase Ti-6Al-4V microstructures, using an enhanced grain graph neural network as a surrogate and Burgers orientation relationship-aware ranking, achieving target properties with high efficiency.
AI.motivation: To enable efficient, property-guided inverse design of polycrystalline microstructures, where graph representations compactly encode grain topology and grain boundary information but generating new microstructures meeting prescribed physical properties remains challenging.
AI.method: A conditional diffusion model performs reverse diffusion under prescribed α-phase volume fraction, elastic modulus, and yield-stress proxy targets. An enhanced grain GNN with grain boundary edge features, learnable node/edge embeddings, and multi-statistic pooling serves as forward surrogate for stress prediction and candidate evaluation. BOR-aware ranking is applied post-generation to improve crystallographic consistency. Generated candidates are validated with finite element analysis.
AI.result: Generated candidates consistently approach prescribed properties across four target regimes including an out-of-envelope target. BOR-aware ranking improves mean BOR consistency by up to 44.9% (in-envelope) and 56.4% (out-of-envelope) while maintaining property alignment. Finite element validation shows max absolute relative error of 1.0% in mean properties. Diffusion requires only 32 candidate evaluations per input graph versus ~40,000 for random/evolutionary search, reducing runtime by ~two orders of magnitude.
AI.conclusion: Conditional grain-graph diffusion is established as an efficient and accurate framework for property-guided polycrystalline microstructure design, significantly outperforming conventional search methods in computational cost while maintaining high property fidelity.

title: Synthesis and structural validation of close-to-stoichiometric NiTe$_2$ single crystals
summary: We report the synthesis of stoichiometric NiTe$_{2}$ single crystals via chemical vapor transport together with precise structural characterization. A combined analysis using powder X-ray diffraction (XRD) and single crystal XRD was performed to determine lattice parameters and structural details. High-resolution single crystal XRD reveals no evidence of interstitial nickel, confirming a close-to-stoichiometric composition. This work establishes a reliable benchmark for the crystal structure of stoichiometric NiTe$_{2}$, offering a reference for future studies on its physical properties.

AI.tldr: The paper reports the synthesis of stoichiometric NiTe2 single crystals via chemical vapor transport, with precise structural characterization using powder and single-crystal X-ray diffraction. High-resolution XRD confirms no interstitial nickel, establishing a reliable structural benchmark for stoichiometric NiTe2.
AI.motivation: To establish a reliable benchmark for the crystal structure of stoichiometric NiTe2, addressing the need for well-characterized reference material for future studies on its physical properties.
AI.method: Synthesis of NiTe2 single crystals via chemical vapor transport, followed by combined powder X-ray diffraction (XRD) and single crystal XRD to determine lattice parameters and structural details. High-resolution single crystal XRD was used to check for interstitial nickel.
AI.result: High-resolution single crystal XRD reveals no evidence of interstitial nickel, confirming a close-to-stoichiometric composition. Lattice parameters and structural details were accurately determined from combined XRD analyses.
AI.conclusion: This work establishes a reliable structural benchmark for stoichiometric NiTe2, providing a reference for future physical property investigations.

title: Band topology and symmetry-driven magneto-optical response in two-dimensional d-wave altermagnets with staggered spin-orbit coupling
summary:
Altermagnets combine compensated collinear magnetic order with momentum-dependent spin splitting, providing a route to transverse electronic and optical responses without a net ferromagnetic moment. We develop a strictly periodic four-band tight-binding model for a two-dimensional d-wave altermagnet and distinguish the roles of three spin orbit coupling (SOC) channels: uniform Rashba SOC, a sublattice-staggered Rashba interaction, and bond-staggered SOC.
  In the absence of SOC, the d-wave kinetic anisotropy produces spin-polarized Dirac points on orthogonal Brillouin-zone boundaries, related by the altermagnetic fourfold spin-group symmetry. Uniform Rashba SOC mixes the spin sectors and shifts these nodes but preserves the antiunitary symmetry that forbids an integrated Hall response. The sublattice-staggered Rashba term breaks this symmetry and activates transverse optical response, whereas the bond-staggered SOC provides the mass that gaps the boundary nodes. Their combined action generates strong Berry-curvature hot spots and, within a narrow parameter window, an isolated lower two-band manifold with Chern number C=-2. For the representative parameters considered here it is possible to stabilize a Chern insulator phase.
  Using covariant-velocity Kubo calculations, we show that large optical Hall conductivity and circular dichroism extend well beyond the nonzero-Chern region and are controlled by SOC-induced avoided crossings and symmetry breaking. We further find that carrier doping strongly modifies the resonant and dc Hall responses through Pauli blocking and the occupation of Berry-curvature hot spots, enabling gate-controlled sign reversals. These results identify the complementary roles of distinct interfacial SOC mechanisms in producing topology and tunable magneto-optical activity in compensated two-dimensional magnets.

AI.tldr: The authors develop a strictly periodic four-band tight-binding model for a 2D d-wave altermagnet, showing that distinct spin-orbit coupling (SOC) channels—uniform Rashba, sublattice-staggered Rashba, and bond-staggered SOC—play complementary roles: uniform Rashba preserves antiunitary symmetry, sublattice-staggered Rashba breaks it to activate transverse optics, and bond-staggered SOC gaps the nodes. Their combined action can produce a Chern insulator (C=-2) and lead to large, tunable optical Hall conductivity and circular dichroism controlled by carrier doping.
AI.motivation: Altermagnets offer transverse electronic and optical responses without a net ferromagnetic moment, but the role of different spin-orbit coupling mechanisms in generating topology and magneto-optical responses in compensated 2D magnets has not been systematically distinguished.
AI.method: A strictly periodic four-band tight-binding model for a 2D d-wave altermagnet is constructed, considering three SOC channels separately. Spin-group symmetry analysis and covariant-velocity Kubo calculations are used to compute Berry curvature, optical Hall conductivity, and circular dichroism as functions of parameters and carrier doping.
AI.result: Uniform Rashba SOC mixes spin sectors but preserves antiunitary symmetry forbidding integrated Hall response; sublattice-staggered Rashba breaks this symmetry and activates transverse optical response; bond-staggered SOC gaps boundary nodes. Their combination yields Berry-curvature hot spots and, in a narrow parameter window, a Chern insulator with C=-2. Large optical Hall conductivity and circular dichroism extend beyond the Chern region, and carrier doping enables gate-controlled sign reversals via Pauli blocking.
AI.conclusion: Distinct interfacial SOC mechanisms play complementary roles in producing topology and tunable magneto-optical activity in compensated two-dimensional magnets, identifying a route to gate-controlled magneto-optical response without a net ferromagnetic moment.

title: High-speed and high-gain graphene photovoltaic phototransistor gated by a van der Waals heterojunction
summary: Two-dimensional (2D) material-based phototransistors offer a unique combination of optical sensing, signal amplification, and logic operation within a single device, yet fundamentally suffering from an inherent gain-speed trade-off. Here, we demonstrate a 2D photovoltaic phototransistor that overcomes this limitation using a MoS2/PtSe2 heterojunction to gate a graphene channel. The ultrafast photovoltaic effect in the heterojunction enables charge separation, yielding ultrahigh photoconductive gain (up to 10^8) in graphene channel via interfacial gating. Besides, the response time (below the instrumental resolution of 550 ns) is governed by carrier transit in graphene channel, enabling simultaneous high speed and high gain. Moreover, broadband photodetection from visible to near-infrared is enabled by the optical properties of the MoS2/PtSe2 heterojunction, with the detectivity exceeding 10^11 Jones. These results establish a new paradigm for high-performance 2D phototransistors by harnessing photovoltaic and photogating effects to overcome the classical gain-speed trade-off.

AI.tldr: A 2D photovoltaic phototransistor using a MoS2/PtSe2 heterojunction to gate a graphene channel achieves ultrahigh photoconductive gain (up to 10^8) and simultaneously fast response times (below 550 ns), overcoming the classical gain-speed trade-off that typically limits 2D phototransistors. The device also provides broadband photodetection from visible to near-infrared with detectivity exceeding 10^11 Jones.
AI.motivation: While 2D material-based phototransistors uniquely combine optical sensing, signal amplification, and logic operation in one device, they fundamentally suffer from an inherent gain-speed trade-off. The goal is to overcome this limitation by decoupling charge separation from carrier transit.
AI.method: A MoS2/PtSe2 heterojunction is used to gate a graphene channel. The photovoltaic effect in the heterojunction enables ultrafast charge separation, while photoconductive gain is achieved through interfacial gating of the graphene channel. The response speed is governed by carrier transit within the graphene channel rather than by slow trap/recombination processes.
AI.result: The device achieves ultrahigh photoconductive gain up to 10^8 with response time below the instrumental resolution of 550 ns, enabling simultaneous high speed and high gain. Broadband photodetection from visible to near-infrared is demonstrated with detectivity exceeding 10^11 Jones.
AI.conclusion: This work establishes a new paradigm for high-performance 2D phototransistors by combining photovoltaic and photogating effects to overcome the classical gain-speed trade-off, potentially enabling applications requiring both high sensitivity and fast response.

title: Gradient expansion approximation of the inhomogeneous electron-gas revisited: Higher-order corrections
summary: In our recently published work (our Ref. 1) we revisited the gradient expansion approximation (GEA) of the interacting electron gas, and recalculated the leading-order contribution$-$with respect to the Wigner-Seitz radius $r_s$$-$to the coefficient $B_{xc}[n]$ of the square of the gradient of the electron density in the high-density and slowly varying limits. That work resolved historical controversies regarding these coefficients and demonstrated that serious misconceptions have led to incorrect constraints being imposed on popular functionals within the generalized gradient approximation (GGA). In the present paper, we extend this calculation to obtain the coefficient of the next-to-leading term, which scales as $r_s \ln(r_s)$ relative to the leading order. First, we establish a systematic framework to evaluate the integral expressions for the $b_{xc}$ coefficient of the leading term ($\sim q^2$) of the density-density response function in the long-wavelength limit ($q \to 0$)$-$a prerequisite for computing $B_{xc}[n]$. The significance of the calculation stems from the proof that the coefficient of this $r_s \ln(r_s)$ term receives no corrections from higher-order diagrammatic expressions. Consequently, our derived value serves as an exact, definitive constraint for future GGA functional development; in the high-density slowly-varying limit, any valid functional must reproduce the exact constraints established in both our previous work and the present paper.

AI.tldr: This paper extends the authors' previous work on the gradient expansion approximation (GEA) of the interacting electron gas by computing the coefficient of the next-to-leading term (scaling as r_s ln(r_s)) in the high-density slowly-varying limit. The authors establish a systematic framework for evaluating the b_xc coefficient of the density-density response function and prove that this coefficient receives no corrections from higher-order diagrammatic expressions, providing exact, definitive constraints for GGA functional development.
AI.motivation: The previous work resolved historical controversies regarding leading-order gradient expansion coefficients of the exchange-correlation energy and corrected incorrect constraints imposed on GGA functionals. This paper extends that calculation to the next-to-leading term, which is motivated by the need to provide exact, definitive constraints for future GGA functional development in the high-density slowly-varying limit.
AI.method: The authors establish a systematic framework to evaluate integral expressions for the b_xc coefficient of the leading term (~q^2) of the density-density response function in the long-wavelength limit (q→0). This is a prerequisite for computing the B_xc[n] coefficient of the gradient expansion. They then compute the coefficient of the next-to-leading term that scales as r_s ln(r_s) relative to leading order, and prove that this coefficient receives no corrections from higher-order diagrammatic expressions.
AI.result: A derived exact value for the r_s ln(r_s) coefficient of the GEA, which is proven to be exact (receiving no corrections from higher-order diagrams), providing definitive constraints for GGA functional development in the high-density slowly-varying limit.
AI.conclusion: The derived coefficient serves as an exact, definitive constraint for future GGA functional development. Any valid functional must reproduce the exact constraints established in both the previous work and this paper when operating in the high-density slowly-varying limit.

title: Charge Tunable Optical Nonlinearity of Moiré Exciton-Polaritons
summary: Transition metal dichalcogenides represent a versatile platform to study strong light-matter interactions based on excitons and electrons in ordered lattices. Twist-engineering of moiré structures further enables the manipulation of the polaritonic nonlinearities via engineering the exciton landscape on the nanoscale. In this work, we demonstrate in-situ control of the optical saturation-based nonlinearity of moiré exciton-polaritons by phase space restriction via charge doping. Strong exciton-photon coupling is established in a gate-controllable MoTe$_2$-MoSe$_2$ heterobilayer, embedded in a spectrally-tunable open cavity. A small gate voltage can effectively lower the necessary polariton density by one order of magnitude to achieve a similar nonlinear saturation effect as in the charge-neutral case. Our microscopic description successfully explains the observed phenomena in the framework of Pauli blocking for the moiré superlattices with charge preoccupation.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates in-situ control of optical saturation-based nonlinearity in moiré exciton-polaritons by charge doping in a gate-controllable MoTe₂-MoSe₂ heterobilayer embedded in a tunable open cavity. A small gate voltage lowers the necessary polariton density by one order of magnitude for the same nonlinear saturation effect, explained by Pauli blocking in charge-preoccupied moiré superlattices.
AI.motivation: Transition metal dichalcogenides and moiré structures offer a versatile platform for strong light-matter interactions, but engineering polaritonic nonlinearities at the nanoscale remains challenging. The authors aim to achieve dynamic, in-situ control of optical nonlinearity in moiré exciton-polaritons via phase space restriction through charge doping.
AI.method: The authors establish strong exciton-photon coupling in a gate-controllable MoTe₂-MoSe₂ heterobilayer embedded in a spectrally-tunable open cavity. They apply small gate voltages to induce charge doping and control the phase space filling of moiré excitons, thereby modulating the saturation-based optical nonlinearity. A microscopic description based on Pauli blocking for charge-preoccupied moiré superlattices is developed to explain the observations.
AI.result: A small gate voltage effectively reduces the required polariton density by one order of magnitude to achieve a nonlinear saturation effect comparable to that in the charge-neutral case. The microscopic model successfully reproduces the observed phenomena within the framework of Pauli blocking for moiré superlattices with charge preoccupation.
AI.conclusion: Charge doping provides an efficient in-situ knob to control the nonlinear optical response of moiré exciton-polaritons, enabling significant enhancement of nonlinearity at reduced polariton densities, with applications for tunable polaritonic devices.

title: A Large-scale Parallel Implementation of Quasi-Four-Component Relativistic Density Functional Theory with Numeric Atom-centered Orbitals
summary: We present a large-scale parallel implementation of fully relativistic density functional theory (DFT) for both molecules and periodic solids, using the quasi-four-component (Q4C) method and numeric atom-centered orbital basis sets. Our approach employs a domain decomposition method on nonuniform real-space integration grids, which enables order-N integration of the Q4C Hamiltonian matrix elements using efficient, distributed-memory and compute-parallel real-space operations. Next, we build the Hamiltonian and overlap matrices in a two-dimensional block-cyclic distribution layout. The resulting generalized eigenvalue problems are solved with the massively parallel ELPA eigenvalue solver library. We benchmark memory usage, parallel efficiency, and scalability across multiple MPI tasks and compute nodes. This algorithm extends the reach of fully relativistic DFT simulations for periodic solids, tested up to 3,383 atoms per unit cell (216,628 basis functions) and likely still well below the true reach of the implementation. As a demonstration, we calculate the fully relativistic band structure for a 3,383 atom-per-unit-cell doped hybrid organic-inorganic perovskite, (PEA)2(Pb1-xBix)I4 (PEA=phenethylammonium), showing nearly ideal scalability between 336 and 672 physical CPU cores.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a large-scale parallel implementation of fully relativistic DFT using the quasi-four-component (Q4C) method with numeric atom-centered orbital basis sets, applicable to both molecules and periodic solids. It employs domain decomposition on nonuniform real-space grids for order-N integration, a block-cyclic distributed Hamiltonian matrix, and the ELPA eigenvalue solver library for massively parallel generalized eigenvalue problems.
AI.motivation: To extend the reach of fully relativistic DFT simulations to large periodic systems, overcoming the computational bottlenecks of relativistic Hamiltonian construction and eigenvalue solving to enable simulations at the scale of thousands of atoms per unit cell.
AI.method: The method combines: (1) quasi-four-component (Q4C) formulation for full relativity, (2) numeric atom-centered orbital basis sets, (3) domain decomposition on nonuniform real-space grids enabling order-N integration of Q4C Hamiltonian matrix elements, (4) distributed-memory parallel real-space operations, (5) twofold block-cyclic distribution of Hamiltonian and overlap matrices, and (6) the massively parallel ELPA eigenvalue solver library.
AI.result: Benchmarks show the implementation handles up to 3,383 atoms per unit cell (216,628 basis functions) for periodic solids. The method demonstrates near-ideal scalability between 336 and 672 physical CPU cores. A demonstration on the doped hybrid organic-inorganic perovskite (PEA)2(Pb1-xBix)I4 yields fully relativistic band structures at this scale.
AI.conclusion: The parallel Q4C implementation substantially extends the reach of fully relativistic DFT to very large periodic systems, with the tested scale likely still well below the true capacity of the implementation.

title: Proximity effects of chiral magnetization on transition metal dichalcogenides monolayers
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures, joint submission with "Valley-controlled chiral magnetism in transition metal dichalcogenide monolayers" by the same authors
summary: We consider the proximity effects of a commensurate chiral $120^{\circ}$ Néel magnetic structure on the transport and optical properties of a transition metal dichalcogenide monolayer (TMD ML). The enlarged magnetic unit cell leads to the folding of the Brillouin zone and enables efficient intervalley spin-flip scattering. Starting from a six band tight binding model, we develop an effective $k\cdot p$ model, which describes the coupling between charge carriers in the TMD ML and the chiral magnetization. We predict the anomalous antiferromagnetic Hall effect (AHE) for conduction electrons and describe it accounting for the interplay between anomalous velocity, side jump, and skew scattering contributions. The proximity of the chiral magnetization also leads to the mixing and splitting of the exciton resonances in the two valleys which are related by the time reversal symmetry despite zero net magnetization. Finally, we demonstrate the possibility to measure the distribution of in-plane orientation of the chiral magnetization through Faraday rotation and the ellipticity of incident linearly polarized light.

AI.tldr: The paper studies the proximity effects of a commensurate chiral 120° Néel magnetic structure on a transition metal dichalcogenide monolayer (TMD ML). Using an effective k·p model derived from a six-band tight-binding model, the authors predict an anomalous antiferromagnetic Hall effect (AHE) for conduction electrons, exciton resonance mixing/splitting across valleys despite zero net magnetization, and demonstrate a way to probe the in-plane chiral magnetization orientation via Faraday rotation and ellipticity measurements.
AI.motivation: To understand how a chiral 120° Néel antiferromagnetic structure, through proximity coupling, modifies the electronic, transport, and optical properties of a TMD monolayer—particularly when there is no net magnetization but the magnetic structure is commensurate and chiral.
AI.method: Starting from a six-band tight-binding model, the authors develop an effective k·p model that captures the coupling between charge carriers in the TMD monolayer and the chiral magnetization. The enlarged magnetic unit cell is handled via Brillouin zone folding, which enables efficient intervalley spin-flip scattering. The Hall effect is analyzed by accounting for anomalous velocity, side jump, and skew scattering contributions. Optical properties are studied via exciton resonance analysis and Faraday rotation/ellipticity calculations.
AI.result: The authors predict an anomalous antiferromagnetic Hall effect (AHE) for conduction electrons driven by the chiral magnetization, and find chirality-induced mixing and splitting of exciton resonances in the two time-reversal-related valleys despite zero net magnetization. They also demonstrate that the in-plane orientation of the chiral magnetization can be measured through Faraday rotation and ellipticity of incident linearly polarized light.
AI.conclusion: Proximity coupling to a commensurate chiral 120° Néel magnetic structure can induce rich transport and optical phenomena in TMD monolayers—including an anomalous antiferromagnetic Hall effect and valley exciton splitting—even in the absence of net magnetization, and provides a route to optically probe the chiral spin texture orientation.

title: Non-relativistic spin splitting in a triangular metal-excess magnet Fe$_{1+δ}$Sb
summary: Non-relativistic spin-splitting (NRSS) antiferromagnets have recently emerged as an important class of magnetic materials that combine compensated magnetism with momentum-dependent spin splitting, offering new opportunities for spintronic applications. Here, we investigate a NiAs-type Fe$_{1+δ}$Sb series ($δ= 0.17$-0.30) using neutron diffraction, pair distribution function, magnetometry and density functional theory calculations. Neutron diffraction establishes that Fe$_{1+δ}$Sb adopts a $120^\circ$ coplanar compensated magnetic order with a non-zero propagation vector $\mathbf{k}=(1/3,\,1/3,\,0)$. Increasing interstitial Fe suppresses the ordered magnetic moment while inducing local symmetry lowering, as revealed by pair distribution function refinements. Density functional theory predicts momentum-dependent spin splitting, dominated by an out-of-plane spin polarization with an odd-parity f-wave-like symmetry, establishing the material as a non-collinear NRSS antiferromagnet. Motivated by the structural similarities between Fe$_{1+δ}$Sb and a known altermagnet CrSb, we further investigate their solid solution and find that Cr substitution at intermediate concentrations gives rise to a ferromagnetic component and a cluster spin-glass behavior. These results establish Fe$_{1+δ}$Sb as a new platform for non-collinear NRSS antiferromagnetism and demonstrate metal interstitial and substitution as effective parameters for tuning the magnetic order and properties.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates NiAs-type Fe₁₊δSb (δ = 0.17–0.30) and establishes it as a non-collinear non-relativistic spin-splitting (NRSS) antiferromagnet. Using neutron diffraction, PDF, magnetometry, and DFT, the authors confirm a 120° coplanar compensated magnetic order with k = (1/3, 1/3, 0), find that interstitial Fe suppresses ordered moment while lowering local symmetry, and predict odd-parity f-wave-like spin splitting with out-of-plane polarization. Cr substitution toward CrSb introduces ferromagnetic components and cluster spin-glass behavior, highlighting interstitial and substitution chemistry as tuning parameters.
AI.motivation: Non-relativistic spin-splitting (NRSS) antiferromagnets represent a new class of magnetic materials combining compensated magnetism with momentum-dependent spin splitting, which could enable novel spintronic applications. The authors aim to identify and characterize new members of this class beyond existing examples.
AI.method: Combined experimental and computational approach: neutron diffraction for magnetic structure determination, pair distribution function (PDF) analysis for local symmetry and interstitial effects, magnetometry for macroscopic magnetic properties, and density functional theory (DFT) calculations to predict electronic spin-splitting character. Additionally, a Fe₁₊δSb–CrSb solid solution was investigated.
AI.result: Fe₁₊δSb exhibits a 120° coplanar compensated magnetic order with propagation vector k = (1/3, 1/3, 0). Increasing δ suppresses the ordered moment and causes local symmetry lowering. DFT predicts momentum-dependent spin splitting dominated by out-of-plane spin polarization with odd-parity f-wave-like symmetry, establishing Fe₁₊δSb as a non-collinear NRSS antiferromagnet. Intermediate Cr substitution induces a ferromagnetic component and cluster spin-glass behavior.
AI.conclusion: Fe₁₊δSb is established as a new platform for non-collinear NRSS antiferromagnetism. Metal interstitial concentration and cation substitution are demonstrated as effective chemical knobs for tuning magnetic ordering and emergent properties.

title: Valley-controlled chiral magnetism in transition metal dichalcogenide monolayers
comment: 7+2 pages, 4+1 figures, joint submission with "Proximity effects of chiral magnetization on transition metal dichalcogenides monolayers" by the same authors
summary: We put forward the Ruderman-Kittel-Kasuya-Yosida (RKKY) interaction in transition metal dichalcogenide monolayers as a tool to create and control a chiral magnetic texture. We show that in the spin-valley locking regime, the RKKY interaction acts as a Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya coupling with an effective spin rotation period exactly equal to the tripled lattice constant. Using mean field theory and classical Monte Carlo simulations, we demonstrate that this interaction qualitatively reshapes the phase diagram of atomically thin antiferromagnets. It destroys the chirality-related phase transition by selecting a single chirality value even when the RKKY interaction is small. At the same time, it shifts the Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless transition associated with spins orientation to higher temperatures. We argue that the valley degree of freedom of electrons mediating the RKKY interaction provides a powerful control knob for exploring non-universal phase transitions and quantum spin liquid states in two-dimensional van der Waals heterostructures.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes using RKKY interaction in transition metal dichalcogenide monolayers to create and control chiral magnetic textures, showing it acts as an effective Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya coupling with a spin rotation period equal to three times the lattice constant, which reshapes the phase diagram of atomically thin antiferromagnets.
AI.motivation: To introduce a new tool for creating and controlling chiral magnetic textures using the valley degree of freedom in TMD monolayers, potentially enabling exploration of non-universal phase transitions and quantum spin liquid states in 2D van der Waals heterostructures.
AI.method: The authors analyze the RKKY interaction in the spin-valley locking regime of TMD monolayers, derive an effective Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya coupling, and use mean-field theory and classical Monte Carlo simulations to study the resulting phase diagram.
AI.result: The RKKY interaction acts as a DM-type coupling with a spin rotation period of triple the lattice constant. It destroys the chirality-related phase transition by selecting a single chirality value even for small RKKY interaction strength, while shifting the Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless transition for spin orientation to higher temperatures.
AI.conclusion: The valley degree of freedom in RKKY-mediated interactions provides a powerful control parameter for tuning chiral magnetism and exploring exotic phase transitions and quantum spin liquid states in 2D van der Waals heterostructures.

title: Spin-chirality-driven nonrelativistic Edelstein effects in two-dimensional antiferromagnets
summary: Charge current-induced magnetic moment accumulation-Edelstein effect has been extensively attracting attention for its promising applications in spintronics. While most prior works focus on the spin-orbit coupling (SOC) induced Edelstein responses that rely on the presence of heavy elements, the nonrelativistic Edelstein effect (in the absence of SOC) that could be applied in a broader material family has been largely unexplored. Here, we perform a combined group-theoretical and ab initio numerical simulation study to show that vector spin chirality could serve as an effective control parameter of nonrelativistic Edelstein responses in antiferromagnetic system. In addition to spin degree of freedom, we also explore the orbital angular momentum contributions to current-induced magnetic moments (dubbed orbital Edelstein effect), which obey distinct symmetry constraints from the spin counterpart. Microscopically, vector spin chirality k gives rise to electronic and Zeeman-like band-geometric quantities, such as the anomalous spin/orbital polarizability and the Berry connection polarizability, which govern the nonrelativistic Edelstein responses. Our work identifies vector spin chirality as a key magnetic order parameter to enable and tune nonrelativistic Edelstein effects, and uncovers a new route toward electrically controlling magnetization without relying on SOC effect.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates via group-theoretical and ab initio calculations that vector spin chirality can serve as a control parameter for nonrelativistic Edelstein effects (both spin and orbital) in antiferromagnetic systems, enabled by electronic and Zeeman-like band-geometric quantities such as anomalous spin/orbital polarizability and Berry connection polarizability, offering a route to electrically control magnetization without spin-orbit coupling.
AI.motivation: Most previous Edelstein effect studies rely on spin-orbit coupling and heavy elements, leaving the nonrelativistic regime (SOC-free) largely unexplored—despite its potential for a broader material family. The authors aim to identify mechanisms and control parameters for SOC-free Edelstein responses.
AI.method: Combined group-theoretical analysis and ab initio numerical simulations applied to antiferromagnetic systems, examining vector spin chirality as an order parameter. Both spin and orbital angular momentum contributions are analyzed, with distinct symmetry constraints identified for each. The responses are traced to anomalous spin/orbital polarizability and Berry connection polarizability.
AI.result: Vector spin chirality k is shown to control nonrelativistic spin and orbital Edelstein effects in antiferromagnets. The orbital Edelstein effect obeys symmetry constraints distinct from the spin counterpart. Both responses are governed microscopically by band-geometric quantities (anomalous spin/orbital polarizability and Berry connection polarizability).
AI.conclusion: Vector spin chirality is a key magnetic order parameter enabling and tuning nonrelativistic Edelstein effects, opening a new route to electrically control magnetization without relying on SOC, thus expanding the applicable spintronics material family.

title: Optical switching of magnetic order in few-layer CrSBr
summary: Manipulating magnetism with light is crucial for both fundamental understanding and technological advancements of information storage devices. The layered antiferromagnet CrSBr, part of the recently emerging class of two-dimensional van der Waals magnets, offers a unique path towards optical control of magnetism via magneto-excitons, which allow optical readout of the spin alignment and also provide a strong absorption channel. Here, we use exciton absorption and photoluminescence to demonstrate optical switching of the magnetic order in bi- and trilayer CrSBr. Using a continuous-wave laser with a power as low as a few microwatts at near-critical external magnetic fields, we demonstrate both local and remote switching of the magnetic configuration in extended lateral domains and further employ this mechanism to deterministically prepare the zero-field magnetic configuration. Our results establish optical switching as a useful means of controlling magnetism in CrSBr, with potential applications in magneto-optoelectronic devices.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates optical switching of magnetic order in bi- and trilayer CrSBr using continuous-wave laser excitation with only a few microwatts of power at near-critical magnetic fields. This enables local and remote switching of magnetic configurations in extended lateral domains and deterministic preparation of the zero-field magnetic configuration, establishing optical control of magnetism in layered antiferromagnetic CrSBr via magneto-excitons.
AI.motivation: Manipulating magnetism with light is essential for both fundamental physics and practical applications in information storage devices. The authors aim to establish a viable means of optical control over magnetism in the emerging 2D van der Waals magnet CrSBr, leveraging its unique magneto-exciton properties for both readout and switching.
AI.method: The authors use exciton absorption and photoluminescence spectroscopy to probe and manipulate the magnetic order in bi- and trilayer CrSBr. They employ a continuous-wave laser with power as low as a few microwatts, applied at near-critical external magnetic fields, to achieve optical switching. This allows both local and remote switching of the magnetic configuration across extended lateral domains, and enables deterministic preparation of the zero-field magnetic state.
AI.result: The authors successfully demonstrate optical switching of the magnetic order in bi- and trilayer CrSBr using microwatt-level continuous-wave laser power. They achieve both local and remote switching of magnetic configurations in extended lateral domains and can deterministically prepare the zero-field magnetic configuration.
AI.conclusion: The results establish optical switching as an effective and low-power means of controlling magnetism in CrSBr, opening potential applications in magneto-optoelectronic and information storage devices based on 2D van der Waals magnets.

title: EBSD and Subtle Crystallographic Differences - A Study of Resolving Interlayer Spacings in Nb-Ni and Nb-Co mu-phases
summary: In ordered intermetallics, slight variations in lattice site occupancy and specific interlayer spacings have been identified as the sources of significant changes in critical resolved shear stress and therefore how a given phase may affect alloy properties. So far, atom positions and lattice site occupancies have traditionally been characterised by high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HR-TEM) and X-ray diffraction (XRD), which are methods that offer either local detail or high statistical significance but not both. Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD), by contrast, provides high spatial resolution across large sample areas and therefore, has the potential to enable the local investigation of interlayer spacing and site lattice occupancy with improved statistical reliability. The objectives of the study are to benchmark EBSDs capability for resolving these subtle features and to correlate them with compositional and mechanical properties. In this case study, we therefore show that EBSD can resolve key crystallographic features of mu-phase intermetallics, specifically interlayer spacings. We combine pattern matching with large-scale dynamical simulations of template libraries guided by XRD based information on lattice parameters. For this, we generate structures that vary in the spacing between triple-layer and Kagome layer and in the site lattice occupancy of the 3a site. This approach successfully predicts the change of interlayer spacing between Kagome and triple layers in Nb-Co and Nb-Ni mu-phases, in good agreement with XRD and HR-TEM.

AI.tldr: This study benchmarks the capability of electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) to resolve subtle crystallographic features — specifically interlayer spacings and lattice site occupancies — in mu-phase intermetallics. By combining pattern matching with large-scale dynamical simulations of template libraries guided by XRD-based lattice parameters, the authors successfully predict interlayer spacing changes between Kagome and triple layers in Nb-Co and Nb-Ni mu-phases, in good agreement with XRD and HR-TEM.
AI.motivation: In ordered intermetallics, slight variations in lattice site occupancy and interlayer spacings cause significant changes in critical resolved shear stress, affecting alloy properties. Traditional characterization methods (HR-TEM and XRD) offer either local detail or statistical significance but not both. EBSD promises high spatial resolution across large areas, motivating the need to benchmark its capability for resolving these subtle structural features with improved statistical reliability.
AI.method: The study combines EBSD pattern matching with large-scale dynamical simulations of template libraries. Structures were generated that vary in the spacing between triple-layer and Kagome layers and in the site lattice occupancy of the 3a site. Template libraries were guided by XRD-based lattice parameter information to resolve the subtle crystallographic features.
AI.result: EBSD successfully resolved key crystallographic features of mu-phase intermetallics, specifically interlayer spacings. The approach correctly predicted the change in interlayer spacing between Kagome and triple layers in both Nb-Co and Nb-Ni mu-phases, showing good agreement with XRD and HR-TEM measurements.
AI.conclusion: EBSD, combined with dynamical simulation-based pattern matching and XRD-guided template libraries, offers a viable and statistically reliable method for locally resolving subtle crystallographic features such as interlayer spacings in intermetallic phases, complementing traditional HR-TEM and XRD approaches.

title: Second-harmonic generation in twisted double bilayer graphene: Double-resonant enhancement from moiré flat bands
summary: We theoretically investigate second-harmonic generation (SHG) in twisted double bilayer graphene (TDBG) with AB--AB and AB--BA stacking configurations using a perturbative approach based on an effective continuum Hamiltonian. We present a systematic analysis of the SHG response as a function of twist angle, vertical bias voltage, Fermi energy, and stacking configuration. We find that the SHG signal is strongly enhanced at small twist angles due to the emergence of moiré flat bands and the associated increase in the joint density of states. Beyond this conventional enhancement mechanism, we demonstrate that the reduced bandwidth enables a pronounced double-resonant process, in which optical transitions at both $ω$ and $2ω$ are simultaneously satisfied over extended regions of the moiré Brillouin zone. This mechanism leads to a substantial amplification of the SHG response, analogous to the enhancement observed in systems with discrete energy levels, but realised here in a tuneable moiré band structure. Furthermore, we show that the AB--AB and AB--BA configurations exhibit a systematic $π$ phase shift in the SHG response at large bias voltages, reflecting their distinct symmetry and electronic structure. Our results identify double-resonance effects as a generic mechanism for enhancing SHG in moiré systems and provide a unified framework for understanding and controlling nonlinear optical responses in tuneable flat-band materials.

AI.tldr: This paper theoretically investigates second-harmonic generation (SHG) in twisted double bilayer graphene (TDBG) with AB-AB and AB-BA stacking, using a perturbative approach based on an effective continuum Hamiltonian. It finds that SHG is strongly enhanced at small twist angles due to moiré flat bands and joint density of states, and more importantly, demonstrates a pronounced double-resonant process where optical transitions at both ω and 2ω are simultaneously satisfied, substantially amplifying SHG. A systematic π phase shift between AB-AB and AB-BA stacking configurations is also shown at large bias voltages.
AI.motivation: To understand and control nonlinear optical responses in tuneable flat-band moiré materials, particularly identifying generic mechanisms (such as double-resonance) that enhance SHG in these systems.
AI.method: Perturbative theoretical approach based on an effective continuum Hamiltonian, systematically analyzing SHG response as a function of twist angle, vertical bias voltage, Fermi energy, and stacking configuration (AB-AB vs AB-BA) in TDBG.
AI.result: SHG is strongly enhanced at small twist angles due to moiré flat bands and increased joint density of states. Reduced bandwidth enables a pronounced double-resonant process with simultaneous optical transitions at ω and 2ω over extended moiré Brillouin zone regions, amplifying SHG substantially. AB-AB and AB-BA configurations exhibit a systematic π phase shift in SHG at large bias voltages.
AI.conclusion: Double-resonance effects represent a generic mechanism for enhancing SHG in moiré systems, and the results provide a unified framework for understanding and controlling nonlinear optical responses in tuneable flat-band materials.

title: Twist-induced magnetic topological phase transition in stacked altermagnetic CrO
summary: Interlayer twisting offers a geometric route to controlling electronic states, but whether it can simultaneously reconstruct magnetic symmetry and band topology remains unclear. Here, based on symmetry analysis and first-principles calculations, we show that commensurate twisting drives magnetic topological phase transitions in stacked bilayer CrO. In particular, it transforms an antiferromagnetic Dirac semimetal into either a $d$-wave altermagnetic bipolarized Weyl semimetal or an unconventional compensated magnetic Weyl semimetal. A key result is that the Weyl points in the $d$-wave altermagnetic phase lie at generic $k$ points in the Brillouin zone and are protected by the spin symmetry $\left\{ C_2 T||C_{2z} T\right\}$. This sharply contrasts with conventional two-dimensional Weyl semimetals, where Weyl points are typically protected by mirror or rotational symmetries and thus pinned to high-symmetry lines. We further show that commensurate twisting preserves the spin symmetry $\left\{ C_2 T||C_{2z} T\right\}$, making the Weyl phase a robust consequence of twisting rather than a fine-tuned feature of a specific angle.
