Our work establishes a symmetry-based route to engineering magnetic topological phases in twisted two-dimensional materials.

AI.tldr: Interlayer twisting drives magnetic topological phase transitions in stacked bilayer CrO, transforming an antiferromagnetic Dirac semimetal into either a d-wave altermagnetic bipolarized Weyl semimetal or an unconventional compensated magnetic Weyl semimetal. The Weyl points are protected by spin symmetry {C2T||C2zT} at generic k points, contrasting with conventional 2D Weyl semimetals where Weyl points are pinned to high-symmetry lines.
AI.motivation: To explore whether interlayer twisting can simultaneously reconstruct magnetic symmetry and band topology in twisted two-dimensional materials, a question that was previously unclear.
AI.method: Symmetry analysis combined with first-principles calculations on commensurately twisted stacked bilayer CrO.
AI.result: Com mensurate twisting drives magnetic topological phase transitions: an antiferromagnetic Dirac semimetal becomes either a d-wave altermagnetic bipolarized Weyl semimetal or an unconventional compensated magnetic Weyl semimetal. Weyl points in the altermagnetic phase lie at generic k points, protected by spin symmetry {C2T||C2zT}, and this spin symmetry is preserved under commensurate twisting, making the Weyl phase robust.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a symmetry-based route to engineering magnetic topological phases in twisted two-dimensional materials, showing that twisting provides a robust geometric control over both magnetic ordering and band topology.

title: Floquet spin-group framework and its application to light-tailored spin splitting in collinear magnets
summary: Altermagnets combine momentum-dependent spin splitting with vanishing net magnetization, opening new opportunities for spintronics. Recent studies have shown that periodic driving by linearly or circularly polarized light, as well as by multicolor light fields, can control spin splitting in altermagnets and conventional antiferromagnets, and can even generate spin splitting patterns absent in equilibrium. Despite this progress, a unified principle connecting the dynamical symmetry of light to the symmetry of spin-split bands remains lacking, limiting the systematic design of light-induced spin structures. Here, by combining the spin group of crystals with the dynamical group of light, we establish a unified Floquet spin group framework for the study of periodically driven collinear magnets with negligible spin-orbit coupling. This framework systematically determines the allowed parity, momentum dependence, and nodal structure of spin splitting under different driving protocols. Guided by this symmetry classification, we show that odd-parity, even-parity, and mixed-parity spin splittings can be switched within the same material by tailoring the driving field. We further uncover higher-order $h$-wave and $k$-wave spin splittings in three-dimensional systems. Our work establishes a unified symmetry framework for light-controlled spin splitting and provides general principles for engineering nonequilibrium spin-band structures in altermagnets and related magnetic materials.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes a unified Floquet spin group framework that combines the spin group of crystals with the dynamical group of light, enabling systematic classification and design of light-induced spin splitting in periodically driven collinear magnets with negligible spin-orbit coupling. This allows switching between odd-parity, even-parity, and mixed-parity spin splittings in the same material and reveals higher-order h-wave and k-wave spin splittings in 3D systems.
AI.motivation: Although prior work has demonstrated that periodic driving by polarized and multicolor light fields can control spin splitting in altermagnets and antiferromagnets, a unified principle connecting the dynamical symmetry of light to the symmetry of spin-split bands is lacking, which limits systematic design of light-induced spin structures.
AI.method: The authors combine the spin group of crystals with the dynamical group of light to construct a unified Floquet spin group framework. This framework systematically determines the allowed parity, momentum dependence, and nodal structure of spin splitting under different driving protocols in periodically driven collinear magnets with negligible spin-orbit coupling.
AI.result: The framework enables switching among odd-parity, even-parity, and mixed-parity spin splittings within the same material by tailoring the driving field, and uncovers higher-order h-wave and k-wave spin splittings in three-dimensional systems.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a unified symmetry framework for light-controlled spin splitting and offers general principles for engineering nonequilibrium spin-band structures in altermagnets and related magnetic materials.

title: Why Ammoniated Lithium Borohydrides Liquefy and Resolidify?
summary: Ammonia ($\mathrm{NH_3}$) absorption drives $\mathrm{LiBH_4}\!\cdot\!x\mathrm{NH_3}$ through a re-entrant "solid-liquid-solid" transition: $\mathrm{LiBH_4\cdot NH_3}$ is a well-defined solid ammoniate, compositions near $\mathrm{LiBH_4\cdot 2NH_3}$ are liquid-like or partially liquefied, whereas $\mathrm{LiBH_4\cdot 3NH_3}$ returns to a more rigid, non-liquid ammoniate state. However, the microscopic origin of this unintuitive response remains a long-lasting mystery. Here, we uncover its mechanism. Cross-database analysis identifies borohydrides as a particularly state-diverse and composition-responsive material family. Structure prediction and ab initio molecular simulations reveal that $\mathrm{NH_3}$ progressively replaces $\mathrm{BH_4^-}$ in the Li coordination shell. The liquid-like state emerges not at the highest $\mathrm{NH_3}$ loading but near $x \approx 2$, where Li-N and Li-B coordination modes are strongly mixed, coordination memory is weakest, and the sampled Li-N/N$\cdots$B coordination landscape is broadest. Further ammoniation produces Li-N-dominant coordination and slows $\mathrm{BH_4^-}/\mathrm{NH_3}$ contact renewal, resulting in increased network persistence and recovery of a rigid ammoniate state. Pressure-composition isotherm, $^1\mathrm{H}$ and $^{11}\mathrm{B}$ nuclear magnetic resonance, and Raman measurements support this non-monotonic state evolution and the associated $\mathrm{BH_4^-}/\mathrm{NH_3}$ reorganization. These findings transform ammonia-induced liquefaction from an empirical phase anomaly into a competition among native-network disruption, mixed-coordination frustration, and ligand-built network reconstruction, providing a framework for chemically switching between transport-favouring fluidity and stability-favouring rigidity in hydrogen-rich materials.

AI.tldr: This paper uncovers the microscopic mechanism behind the re-entrant "solid-liquid-solid" transition in LiBH₄·xNH₃ upon ammonia absorption. The liquid-like state emerges near x≈2 where Li-N and Li-B coordination modes are strongly mixed and coordination memory is weakest, rather than at the highest NH₃ loading. Further ammoniation leads to Li-N-dominant coordination and recovery of a rigid ammoniate state.
AI.motivation: The re-entrant solid-liquid-solid transition in LiBH₄·xNH₃ ammoniates (where solid ammoniate → liquid-like → solid ammoniate as NH₃ loading increases) has remained mechanistically unexplained for a long time. Understanding this non-monotonic state evolution is crucial for controlling fluidity versus rigidity in hydrogen-rich materials.
AI.method: The authors combine a cross-database analysis identifying borohydrides as state-diverse materials, structure prediction, and ab initio molecular simulations to trace how NH₃ progressively replaces BH₄⁻ in the Li coordination shell. They validate findings with pressure-composition isotherm measurements, ¹H and ¹¹B nuclear magnetic resonance, and Raman spectroscopy.
AI.result: The liquid-like state occurs near x≈2 where Li-N and Li-B coordination modes are strongly mixed, coordination memory is weakest, and the Li-N/N⋯B coordination landscape is broadest. At higher NH₃ loading (x≈3), Li-N-dominant coordination slows BH₄⁻/NH₃ contact renewal, increasing network persistence and restoring rigidity. Experimental measurements support this non-monotonic evolution.
AI.conclusion: The work transforms ammonia-induced liquefaction from an empirical phase anomaly into a mechanistic competition among native-network disruption, mixed-coordination frustration, and ligand-built network reconstruction. This framework enables chemically switching between transport-favouring fluidity and stability-favouring rigidity in hydrogen-rich materials.

title: Discrete states and ballistic interference in quantum wires approaching macroscopic lengths
summary: Increasing the size of a system showing quantum effects is a difficult task limited by decoherence, a diminishing quantum level spacing, and the effects of disorder spoiling the quantum behavior when growing in size. Systems in 1D offer very strong confinement in the transverse directions, thus generally enhancing quantum effects, but are notoriously sensitive to disorder. In this work, we present a system of 1D electrons exhibiting discrete quantum levels and fully ballistic coherent quantum interference with lengths of up to 18\,$μ$m. Tunneling spectroscopy between two parallel quantum wires with a central gated segment shows intricate interference patterns exhibiting several different periods in magnetic field and density. An analysis over three different wire lengths and a comparison with single particle numerical simulations without any free parameters remarkably explains the full pattern including the observed periods. Therefore, these wires are essentially ideal 1D systems with aspect ratios approaching 1'000. In addition, at low bias, we also observe not only the Coulomb charging energies but can clearly resolve the discrete orbital and spin states in up to 10\,$μ$m long wires when filling 100 electrons with the center gate. This is made visible by a state-of-the-art low temperature and low noise measurement system. The spin filling sequence is completely regular, strictly alternating spin up and down, avoiding high spin states, while the peak conductance is modulated in accordance with the previously discussed interference patterns. These striking results show that single particle Schrödinger quantum mechanics such as ballistic quantum interference and discrete quantum states may be observed, under the right conditions, in systems of up to 18\,$μ$m length, thus approaching macroscopic sizes.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that 1D electron systems in quantum wires can exhibit fully ballistic coherent quantum interference and discrete quantum levels over lengths up to 18 μm, with aspect ratios approaching 1,000, essentially behaving as ideal 1D systems despite the usual sensitivity to disorder.
AI.motivation: Scaling up quantum systems is fundamentally limited by decoherence, diminishing quantum level spacing, and disorder effects. While 1D systems enhance quantum effects through strong transverse confinement, they are notoriously sensitive to disorder. The authors aim to show that under the right conditions, single-particle quantum mechanics can be observed in systems approaching macroscopic sizes.
AI.method: The authors use tunneling spectroscopy between two parallel quantum wires with a central gated segment. They analyze interference patterns across three different wire lengths and compare results with single-particle numerical simulations without free parameters. Measurements are performed using a state-of-the-art low-temperature, low-noise measurement system to resolve discrete orbital and spin states.
AI.result: The system exhibits discrete quantum levels and fully ballistic coherent quantum interference over lengths up to 18 μm. Interference patterns show multiple periods in magnetic field and density, fully explained by parameter-free single-particle simulations. At low bias, Coulomb charging energies and discrete orbital/spin states are resolved in wires up to 10 μm long with 100 electrons filled. The spin filling sequence alternates strictly between up and down, avoiding high-spin states, with peak conductance modulated by the interference patterns.
AI.conclusion: Single-particle Schrödinger quantum mechanics—including ballistic quantum interference and discrete quantum states—can be observed in systems up to 18 μm long under the right conditions, demonstrating that quantum behavior can be preserved at near-macroscopic length scales in ideal 1D systems.

title: Performance of Tkatchenko-Scheffler Dispersion Method with Updated van der Waals Radii: Importance for Alkali-Containing Systems
comment: The following article has been submitted to the Journal of Chemical Physics
summary: The Tkatchenko-Scheffler (TS) pairwise method to calculate dispersion interactions is a widely used approach to incorporate missing long-range van der Waals contributions in semilocal and hybrid density functional calculations. Despite numerous refinements of the approach to include many-body terms, the original formulation still remains highly relevant as an efficient and robust method, especially for organic and/or insulating materials. In 2018, Fedorov et al. reported updated van der Waals radii to the seminal work published in 2009. The present work examines the accuracy of the TS method with updated van der Waals radii (abbreviated as TS_2018), coupled with the semilocal Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof density functional, for structural predictions of semiconducting and insulating materials in comparison to the non-local many-body dispersion method and the original TS method (TS_2009). Special attention is paid to materials containing alkali elements, for which the TS_2009 method exhibits a large overbinding, associated with potentially large errors in predicted atomic structures. We also consider a more narrow reformulation (TS_alkali) where only the the alkali atoms are corrected, so the method remains otherwise compatible with TS_2009. The binding energy curves of five alkali dimers are used to assess the TS_2009 and the TS_2018 methods in comparison to the random phase approximation. Using 45 inorganic solid compounds with available experimental reference data, as well as three widely studied, Cs-containing halide perovskites, CsPb$X_3$ ($X$ = Cl, Br, I), we then examine the performance of the TS_2018 and TS_alkali approaches compared to TS_2009 and the beyond-pairwise, nonlocal many-body dispersion method; the latter found to give good results as well.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates the accuracy of the Tkatchenko-Scheffler (TS) dispersion method with updated van der Waals radii (TS_2018) and a partial correction (TS_alkali) coupled with the PBE functional, for structural predictions of semiconducting and insulating materials, particularly alkali-containing systems where the original TS_2009 overbinds.
AI.motivation: The TS pairwise method is widely used for dispersion interactions in DFT calculations, but the original TS_2009 exhibits large overbinding for alkali-containing materials, leading to potentially large errors in predicted structures. This work aims to assess whether updated van der Waals radii (TS_2018) improve accuracy.
AI.method: The authors compare TS_2018 and a narrowed TS_alkali reformulation (correcting only alkali atoms, otherwise compatible with TS_2009) against TS_2009 and the nonlocal many-body dispersion method, coupled with the PBE functional. They use binding energy curves of five alkali dimers benchmarked against random phase approximation, 45 inorganic solid compounds with experimental reference data, and three Cs-containing halide perovskites (CsPbX3, X = Cl, Br, I).
AI.result: The accuracy of TS_2018 and TS_alkali is examined against TS_2009 and the beyond-pairwise many-body dispersion method. The many-body dispersion method is found to give good results as well.
AI.conclusion: The updated TS_2018 radii and the partial TS_alkali correction offer improved approaches over TS_2009 for structural predictions in alkali-containing semiconducting and insulating materials, with the many-body dispersion method serving as a reliable beyond-pairwise reference.

title: Comparison of Lindblad and circuit approaches for quantum heat transport
summary: We compare two popular models applicable to analyzing heat transport by thermal microwave photons in quantum circuits. The first model is derived from a weak-coupling Lindblad master equation, with transition rates determined by Fermi's golden rule induced by thermal dissipation sources. The second approach employs a circuit model, where thermal Johnson-Nyquist noise generated by dissipative elements introduces currents, and consequently Joule power, in other parts of the circuit. This leads to a Landauer type expression of heat transport where the transmission coefficient is proportional to the transconductance in the circuit. We find that the two models yield identical results in a linear circuit in the weak coupling limit with an analytic expression of power in an archetypal circuit of a cavity mediating heat between two baths. Our analysis yields a quantitative assessment of the range of validity of the weak coupling assumption in a circuit. Due to the correspondence of the two results, we feel confident in applying the weak coupling Lindblad model also for analyzing heat transport in quantum circuits consisting, e.g. of qubits and/or non-linear resonators.

AI.tldr: The paper compares two models for heat transport by thermal microwave photons in quantum circuits: a weak-coupling Lindblad master equation approach and a Landauer-type circuit model based on Johnson-Nyquist noise. The two models yield identical results in linear circuits within the weak coupling limit, providing a quantitative assessment of the validity of the weak coupling assumption and justifying its use for quantum circuits with qubits and non-linear resonators.
AI.motivation: To determine whether a weak-coupling Lindblad master equation model (based on Fermi's golden rule transition rates) and a circuit-based Landauer approach (based on Johnson-Nyquist noise and Joule power) give consistent descriptions of heat transport by thermal microwave photons in quantum circuits, and to establish the range of validity of the weak coupling assumption.
AI.method: Two models are compared: (1) a Lindblad master equation with Fermi's golden rule transition rates induced by thermal dissipation sources; (2) a circuit model where thermal Johnson-Nyquist noise from dissipative elements generates currents and Joule power, yielding a Landauer-type heat transport expression with transmission coefficient proportional to transconductance. An analytic expression for power is derived for an archetypal cavity-mediated heat transport circuit between two baths.
AI.result: The two models produce identical results in a linear circuit within the weak coupling limit, yielding an analytic expression for power in a cavity-mediated heat transport circuit. The analysis provides a quantitative estimate of the range of validity of the weak coupling assumption in such circuits.
AI.conclusion: Based on the correspondence between the two models, the authors conclude that the weak-coupling Lindblad model can be confidently applied to analyze heat transport in quantum circuits containing qubits and/or non-linear resonators, where the circuit model is less straightforward.

title: Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Sparse Strain-Field Reconstruction in 4D-STEM
comment: 18 pages, 7 figures, 1 table, and Supplementary Material. Code and processed data are available at https://github.com/rmsreis/pinns-4dstem
summary: Quantitative strain mapping using four-dimensional scanning transmission electron microscopy (4D-STEM) typically requires densely sampled scans that can damage beam-sensitive specimens. We develop a physics-informed neural network (PINN) for sparse 4D-STEM strain reconstruction that embeds elastic equilibrium and Saint-Venant compatibility in the training loss through automatic differentiation. The architecture combines a coordinate-based implicit representation, sine activations with stable second derivatives, frozen residual-scale normalization, an exponential physics-weight ramp, and residual-based adaptive collocation. We apply a sine-activated residual network to an experimental $180\times400$-pixel strain map of domain-structured PbGeSnSe$_{1.5}$Te$_{1.5}$. Across $1$-$75%$ sampling ($720$-$54{,}000$ probe positions), $R^2$ for $\varepsilon_{xx}$ reaches $0.80$ at $10%$ sampling and saturates near $0.86$ by $25%$; the chevron strain-band morphology is recovered from $10%$ of probe positions. At $10%$ sampling, the PINN reduces mean absolute error by approximately $26%$ relative to compressed sensing and $22%$ relative to Gaussian-process regression. An ablation against an equal-capacity data-only SIREN shows that the PDE prior improves accuracy at extreme sparsity and consistently improves physical self-consistency, but biases the reconstruction when data are abundant. Monte Carlo dropout and mean-field variational inference provide per-pixel epistemic uncertainty maps correlated with reconstruction error. With an appropriate constitutive model, the framework is adaptable to strain mapping across diverse material systems.

AI.tldr: A physics-informed neural network (PINN) embeds elastic equilibrium and Saint-Venant compatibility constraints for sparse 4D-STEM strain reconstruction, achieving R² ≈ 0.80 at 10% sampling and recovering chevron strain-band morphology in PbGeSnSe₁.₅Te₁.₅ while outperforming compressed sensing and Gaussian-process regression.
AI.motivation: 4D-STEM strain mapping requires dense scanning that damages beam-sensitive specimens. Reducing the number of probe positions is desirable but sparse data alone yields poor reconstructions; physics-based priors can compensate for missing information.
AI.method: The PINN uses a coordinate-based implicit neural representation with a sine-activated residual network. Elastic equilibrium and Saint-Venant compatibility are enforced in the training loss via automatic differentiation. Additional components include stable second-derivative sine activations, frozen residual-scale normalization, an exponential physics-weight ramp, and residual-based adaptive collocation. Per-pixel epistemic uncertainty is estimated via Monte Carlo dropout and mean-field variational inference.
AI.result: Across 1-75% sampling on a 180×400-pixel experimental strain map of PbGeSnSe₁.₅Te₁.₅, R² for εxx reaches 0.80 at 10% sampling and saturates near 0.86 by 25%. The chevron strain-band morphology is recovered from 10% of probe positions. At 10% sampling, the PINN reduces mean absolute error by ~26% vs compressed sensing and ~22% vs Gaussian-process regression. Ablation shows the PDE prior improves accuracy at extreme sparsity and physical self-consistency but biases reconstruction with abundant data.
AI.conclusion: The physics-informed framework enables accurate sparse 4D-STEM strain reconstruction with reliable uncertainty quantification, and is adaptable to other material systems given an appropriate constitutive model.

title: Strain engineering of transient exciton diffusion in WSe2 monolayers at cryogenic temperatures
summary: Tungsten-based transition metal dichalcogenides exhibit dark excitons as the energetically lowest states. These are crucial for exciton thermalization and propagation and they dominate low-temperature photoluminescence via the emergence of pronounced phonon sidebands. After a resonant excitation, highly mobile hot dark excitons are formed, which quickly thermalize into an equilibrium distribution. The application of strain modifies the exciton energy landscape and, in particular, the relative energy separation between bright and dark exciton states. The impact of strain on the transient photoluminescence and diffusion of non-equilibrium excitons has remained largely unexplored so far. In this work, we investigate the spatiotemporal exciton dynamics in strained hBN-encapsulated WSe2 monolayers at cryogenic temperatures. We demonstrate that tensile strain abruptly increases the excess energy of hot excitons, thereby accelerating their transient diffusion. We trace this back to suppressed phonon-mediated scattering from bright to dark excitons. Furthermore, we predict a periodic modulation of the transient exciton diffusion in the presence of a compressive strain resulting from strain-driven emission of M phonons. The gained microscopic insights illustrate how strain can be used to engineer transient photoluminescence and exciton diffusion in technologically promising 2D semiconductors.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates spatiotemporal exciton dynamics in strained hBN-encapsulated WSe2 monolayers at cryogenic temperatures, demonstrating that tensile strain increases hot exciton excess energy and accelerates transient diffusion by suppressing phonon-mediated bright-to-dark scattering, while compressive strain can induce periodic modulation of diffusion via strain-driven M phonon emission—showing strain as a tool to engineer exciton transport in 2D semiconductors.
AI.motivation: While strain is known to modify the exciton energy landscape and the bright-dark exciton separation in WSe2 monolayers, the impact of strain on transient photoluminescence and non-equilibrium exciton diffusion has remained largely unexplored.
AI.method: The authors study strained hBN-encapsulated WSe2 monolayers at cryogenic temperatures, investigating spatiotemporal exciton dynamics through transient photoluminescence measurements combined with theoretical analysis of exciton diffusion under both tensile and compressive strain conditions.
AI.result: Tensile strain abruptly increases the excess energy of hot excitons, accelerating their transient diffusion due to suppressed phonon-mediated scattering from bright to dark excitons. Additionally, compressive strain is predicted to produce a periodic modulation of transient exciton diffusion resulting from strain-driven emission of M phonons.
AI.conclusion: Strain can be used as an effective means to engineer transient photoluminescence and exciton diffusion in technologically promising 2D semiconductors, offering microscopic insights into controlling exciton thermalization and transport.

title: Thermal Stability of Two-Dimensional Crystals with Extended OH Hydrogen-Bonded Chains
summary: Numerical simulations of the dynamics of monolayer structures of molecules deposited on a sheet of hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN) have been performed. It is shown that molecules containing benzene rings and hydroxyl groups in their structure can form stable two-dimensional crystals with linear chains of hydrogen bonds OH$\cdots$OH$\cdots$OH$\cdots$ Such structures are formed by the following molecules: phenol (C$_6$H$_5$OH), hydroquinone (C$_6$H$_4$(OH)$_2$), 4-phenylphenol (C$_6$H$_5$--C$_6$H$_4$OH), 4-(4-phenylphenyl)phenol (C$_6$H$_5$--C$_6$H$_4$--C$_6$H$_4$OH), paracetamol (CH$_3$C(O)NHC$_6$H$_4$OH), 4-hydroxybenzanilide (C$_6$H$_5$C(O)NHC$_6$H$_4$OH) and 4,4-dihydroxybenzanilide (C$_6$H$_4$OHC(O)NHC$_6$H$_4$OH). On the one hand, the benzene rings in these molecules ensure their strong interaction with the flat substrate; on the other hand, they do not hinder the formation of extended hydrogen-bonded chains. The monolayer structures of these molecules exhibit high thermal stability: the onset melting temperatures of their 2D crystals are 47, 187, 127, 247, 167, 307, and 377 $^\circ$C, respectively. The simulations allow us to conclude that multilayer structures composed of h-BN sheets and molecules of hydroquinone, paracetamol, and 4-hydroxybenzanilide can be used for the development of novel proton-exchange membranes capable of operating at elevated temperatures.

AI.tldr: Numerical simulations of molecular monolayers on h-BN show that seven molecules containing benzene rings and hydroxyl groups form stable 2D crystals via linear hydrogen-bond chains (OH···OH···OH), with high thermal stability (onset melting temperatures 47–377 °C). Multilayer structures of h-BN with hydroquinone, paracetamol, and 4-hydroxybenzanilide show promise for high-temperature proton-exchange membranes.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether molecules with both benzene rings (for strong substrate interaction) and hydroxyl groups (for hydrogen bonding) can form stable two-dimensional crystalline monolayers on hexagonal boron nitride, and to explore their potential as building blocks for proton-exchange membranes operating at elevated temperatures.
AI.method: Numerical molecular dynamics simulations of monolayer structures of seven molecules (phenol, hydroquinone, 4-phenylphenol, 4-(4-phenylphenyl)phenol, paracetamol, 4-hydroxybenzanilide, and 4,4-dihydroxybenzanilide) deposited on an h-BN sheet. The simulations focused on the formation of 2D crystals with linear H-bond chains and assessed thermal stability through onset melting temperatures of the 2D crystals.
AI.result: All seven molecules form stable 2D crystals with linear OH···OH···OH hydrogen-bonded chains while maintaining strong benzene ring–substrate interactions. Onset melting temperatures of the 2D crystals were determined as 47, 187, 127, 247, 167, 307, and 377 °C for phenol, hydroquinone, 4-phenylphenol, 4-(4-phenylphenyl)phenol, paracetamol, 4-hydroxybenzanilide, and 4,4-dihydroxybenzanilide, respectively.
AI.conclusion: Benzene-containing hydroxylated molecules can form thermally stable hydrogen-bonded 2D crystals on h-BN. Multilayer h-BN/molecule structures based on hydroquinone, paracetamol, and 4-hydroxybenzanilide are viable candidates for developing novel proton-exchange membranes capable of operating at elevated temperatures.

title: Dual-Mode Exciton Coupling in Epitaxially Registered Organic-Inorganic 2D Heterocrystals
summary: Two-dimensional (2D) heterocrystals comprising molecules and semiconductors can serve as an ideal platform for studying interfacial excitons and for future optoelectronic applications, yet the energy and charge flow across these atomically sharp interfaces remain unclear. In this work, we investigated PTCDA-MoS2 as a prototypical 2D organic-inorganic heterostructure and revealed dual-mode exciton coupling between the constituent crystals. Monolayer-resolved PTCDA molecular crystals were grown on monolayer MoS2 via physical vapor assembly, and their crystallographic details, including the stacking angle, were determined by electron diffraction. Upon the formation of the heterostructures, PTCDA's photoluminescence was completely quenched because of organic-to-inorganic hole transfer, whereas that of MoS2 increased markedly with PTCDA thickness. Using differential reflectance and photoluminescence excitation spectroscopy, we found that the enhancement arises from two distinct mechanisms. Ground-state charge transfer injects holes into MoS2, which suppresses negative trion formation and enhances the radiative recombination of neutral excitons. In addition, resonant energy transfer, enabled by spectral overlap between PTCDA and MoS2, diverts excitation energy from PTCDA to MoS2. Our findings reconcile previously proposed mechanisms and establish a unified framework in which charge and energy transfer cooperate to govern exciton coupling at organic-inorganic interfaces.

AI.tldr: This work investigates a prototypical 2D organic-inorganic heterostructure (PTCDA on monolayer MoS2) and reveals two cooperating mechanisms—ground-state charge transfer (hole injection into MoS2 suppressing trion formation) and resonant energy transfer (spectral-overlap-driven excitation diversion from PTCDA to MoS2)—that together govern exciton coupling at the atomically sharp interface.
AI.motivation: To understand the energy and charge flow across atomically sharp 2D organic-inorganic heterointerfaces, which remains unclear despite their promise for studying interfacial excitons and future optoelectronic applications.
AI.method: Physical vapor assembly of monolayer-resolved PTCDA on monolayer MoS2; crystallographic characterization via electron diffraction (including stacking angle); optical characterization using photoluminescence, differential reflectance, and photoluminescence excitation spectroscopy to disentangle the mechanisms of exciton enhancement.
AI.result: PTCDA photoluminescence was completely quenched due to organic-to-inorganic hole transfer, while MoS2 photoluminescence increased with PTCDA thickness. Two distinct mechanisms were identified: (1) ground-state charge transfer injects holes into MoS2, suppressing negative trion formation and enhancing neutral exciton radiative recombination; (2) resonant energy transfer via spectral overlap diverts excitation energy from PTCDA to MoS2.
AI.conclusion: Charge and energy transfer cooperate at organic-inorganic interfaces, providing a unified framework that reconciles previously proposed mechanisms for exciton coupling in 2D heterostructures.

title: Magnetic Skyrmion Interacting with Optical Skyrmion
summary: Magnetic skyrmions (MSks) and optical skyrmions (OSks) embody topology in matter and in light, respectively. Here we investigate the interaction between a single MSk and an OSk beam. Three distinct nonlinear dynamical modes are identified: rotation, skipping, and trochoidal motion. By decomposing the optical driving force into gradient, orbital-angular-momentum, and spin-angular-momentum contributions, we clarify their respective roles of radial confinement, azimuthal drift, and precessional modulation. The skipping motion arises from the azimuthal asymmetry of the OSk beam and exhibits spatial selectivity originating from the magnetization-polarization coupling between the MSk and OSk. In three dimensions, the coupling acquires a propagation-dependent phase dominated by the differential Gouy phase, which yields $z$-asymmetric skipping trajectories. These results bridge topological particles and topological fields within a unified framework, offering helicity-selective and phase-programmable routes to optomagnonic control.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the interaction between a single magnetic skyrmion (MSk) and an optical skyrmion (OSk) beam, identifying three distinct nonlinear dynamical modes (rotation, skipping, trochoidal motion) and clarifying the roles of gradient, OAM, and SAM force contributions. The skipping motion arises from azimuthal asymmetry and shows z-asymmetric trajectories in 3D due to differential Gouy phase, bridging topological particles and fields in a unified optomagnonic control framework.
AI.motivation: To unify topological matter (magnetic skyrmions) and topological light (optical skyrmions) by studying their mutual interaction, and to understand the underlying force mechanisms so as to enable new routes for optomagnonic control.
AI.method: The optical driving force is decomposed into gradient, orbital-angular-momentum, and spin-angular-momentum contributions, each mapped to radial confinement, azimuthal drift, and precessional modulation respectively. Dynamical modes are classified as rotation, skipping, and trochoidal motion, with 3D coupling analyzed via propagation-dependent (differential Gouy) phase.
AI.result: Three distinct nonlinear dynamical modes (rotation, skipping, trochoidal) are identified. Skipping motion is shown to originate from azimuthal asymmetry of the OSk beam with magnetization-polarization coupling spatial selectivity. In 3D, differential Gouy phase dominates to yield z-asymmetric skipping trajectories.
AI.conclusion: The work bridges topological particles and topological fields in a unified framework, providing helicity-selective and phase-programmable approaches to optomagnonic control.

title: Machine Learning Assisted Design of Complex and High Entropy Alloys by Hybrid HiPIMS/Pulsed-DC PVD Process for Low Carbon Energy Applications in Extreme Environments
summary:
Complex and high entropy alloys are attracting much attention currently thanks to their mechanical and corrosion resistance properties in harsh environments, in particular needed for carbon-free energy applications. However, their elaboration in bulk and in thin film form in a trial-and-error approach is impractical due to their complexity and the cocktail effect. The recent development of artificial intelligence brings a new possibility for their elaboration and adjustment of their properties.
  Firstly, we present an overview of Materials and data science research. Then we describe how DIADEM - French initiative for Materials and Data science convergence - tackles the development of innovative coatings for carbon-free energy applications (nuclear, high temperature electrolysis, ...) thanks to the development of a nationwide network of synthesis and characterization platforms - the DIADEM discovery hub. We describe in particular DIADEM-2D, an AI-driven Hybrid HiPIMS/Pulsed-DC PVD process using 4 cathodes in confocal combinatorial configuration. We present the high entropy alloy determination using data from the literature for corrosion resistance in molten salt media and nuclear accidental conditions. An element-independent model gathering deposition parameters and coating properties has been implemented allowing the design of protective coatings with a particular composition. We demonstrate the feasibility of this process and its accuracy.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces DIADEM, a French national initiative combining Materials Science and Data Science, and presents DIADEM-2D, an AI-driven combinatorial HiPIMS/Pulsed-DC PVD process with 4 cathodes for developing high-entropy alloy protective coatings for carbon-free energy applications (nuclear, high-temperature electrolysis). An element-independent AI model linking deposition parameters to coating properties enables data-driven design of corrosion-resistant coatings in molten salt and nuclear accident conditions.
AI.motivation: Complex and high entropy alloys offer promising mechanical and corrosion resistance properties for harsh environments needed in carbon-free energy applications, but their development through traditional trial-and-error approaches is impractical due to their compositional complexity and the cocktail effect. Artificial intelligence offers a new pathway to accelerate their design and property optimization.
AI.method: The authors describe the DIADEM (French initiative for Materials and Data Science convergence) approach: a nationwide network of synthesis and characterization platforms forming the DIADEM discovery hub. Specifically, they present DIADEM-2D, an AI-driven hybrid HiPIMS/Pulsed-DC PVD process using 4 cathodes in confocal combinatorial configuration. High entropy alloy compositions for corrosion resistance in molten salt and nuclear accident conditions are determined using literature data, and an element-independent model correlating deposition parameters with coating properties is implemented.
AI.result: The paper demonstrates the feasibility and accuracy of the AI-driven combinatorial PVD process for designing protective high-entropy alloy coatings with targeted compositions and properties, validated for corrosion resistance applications in harsh energy environments.
AI.conclusion: The convergence of materials science and data science through initiatives like DIADEM, coupled with AI-driven combinatorial synthesis and element-independent predictive modeling, provides an efficient and accurate pathway for the design and elaboration of high-entropy alloy protective coatings for carbon-free energy applications.

title: Resonantly-enhanced Raman response in graphene-capped bismuthene on SiC
summary: Two-dimensional quantum spin Hall insulators based on atomic monolayers offer a promising route toward dissipationless electronics, yet their practical use is often limited by environmental instability. Encapsulating the system with a graphene capping layer has been shown to be a reliable method to prevent oxidation and degradation. However, the confirmation of a successful encapsulation still relies on ultra-high vacuum techniques, that considerably slow the process. Here, we present an ex situ, rapid, nondestructive and spatially resolved Raman characterization of graphene-capped bismuthene, a honeycomb monolayer of Bi on SiC. A pronounced Raman scattering peak at around 122 cm-1 is identified as the E2g phonon of bismuthene, via a comparison with density functional perturbation theory calculations. We use excitation-energy and polarization-dependent Raman measurements to enable an unambiguous assignment of the spectral features. Tuning the excitation energy close to the excitonic transition in pristine bismuthene, we observe a strong enhancement of the Raman response and the emergence of additional scattering peaks. In this regime, higher-order phonon features, as well as interfacial modes between bismuthene and the SiC substrate, become visible, suggesting the involvement of resonant scattering processes. Our results establish Raman micro-spectroscopy as a versatile tool for probing graphene-protected quantum materials, providing access to lattice dynamics and interlayer coupling.

AI.tldr: Raman micro-spectroscopy is demonstrated as an ex situ, rapid, nondestructive, and spatially resolved probe for graphene-capped bismuthene (a 2D quantum spin Hall insulator). The E2g phonon of bismuthene at ~122 cm⁻¹ is identified and confirmed via density functional perturbation theory, excitation-energy, and polarization-dependent measurements. Resonant excitation near the excitonic transition reveals higher-order phonon and interfacial modes, establishing Raman as a versatile tool for probing graphene-protected quantum materials.
AI.motivation: 2D quantum spin Hall insulators based on atomic monolayers are promising for dissipationless electronics, but environmental instability limits their practical use. Graphene capping prevents oxidation, yet verifying successful encapsulation currently relies on ultra-high vacuum techniques that slow the process. A rapid, ex situ, nondestructive method to characterize these encapsulated systems is needed.
AI.method: The authors perform ex situ Raman micro-spectroscopy on graphene-capped bismuthene (Bi monolayer on SiC). They identify the E2g phonon of bismuthene (~122 cm⁻¹) by comparing with density functional perturbation theory calculations. Excitation-energy-dependent and polarization-dependent Raman measurements enable unambiguous spectral assignments, and tuning excitation close to the excitonic transition of pristine bismuthene reveals resonant enhancement and additional higher-order/interfacial scattering features.
AI.result: A pronounced Raman peak at ~122 cm⁻¹ is assigned to the E2g phonon of bismuthene. Under near-resonant excitation, strong Raman enhancement and additional higher-order phonon features and interfacial modes between bismuthene and the SiC substrate emerge, indicating resonant scattering processes. The method successfully provides lattice dynamics and interlayer coupling information in a rapid, ex situ manner.
AI.conclusion: Raman micro-spectroscopy is established as a versatile, rapid, nondestructive, and spatially resolved tool for probing graphene-protected quantum materials, offering access to lattice dynamics and interlayer coupling without requiring ultra-high vacuum conditions.

title: Exciton-induced magnons carrying orbital angular momentum in CrI3
summary: Magnons are collective spin excitations that contain and transport spin angular momentum in magnetic materials. It has been suggested that they can also carry orbital angular momentum in analogy to the electronic motion around the nucleus. We explore the real-space topology of magnon wave-packets emanating from atomic-like excitons in the ferromagnetic insulator CrI3 and demonstrate the existence of orbital angular momentum in such wave-packets. We reveal that orbital angular momentum of magnons is nearly equal to their spin angular momentum and compensates the latter. This illustrates the existence of an unexplored internal angular momentum balance and demonstrates that the magnetization can be quenched without the need of angular momentum exchange with the lattice.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates that magnons in the ferromagnetic insulator CrI3 can carry orbital angular momentum in addition to spin angular momentum, with the orbital component nearly canceling the spin component, revealing an internal angular momentum balance that allows magnetization quenching without lattice angular momentum exchange.
AI.motivation: To explore whether magnons can carry orbital angular momentum analogous to electronic orbital motion, and to understand the internal angular momentum balance in magnetic systems, which has implications for magnetization dynamics and spintronics.
AI.method: The authors investigate the real-space topology of magnon wave-packets originating from atomic-like excitons in the ferromagnetic insulator CrI3, analyzing their orbital and spin angular momentum contributions.
AI.result: The orbital angular momentum of magnons is found to be nearly equal in magnitude to their spin angular momentum but opposite in sign, effectively compensating the spin contribution.
AI.conclusion: The existence of an internal angular momentum balance between spin and orbital contributions in magnons implies that magnetization can be quenched without requiring angular momentum exchange with the lattice, opening a new avenue for understanding magnetization dynamics.

title: Transient Ferromagnetism in Ultrafast Phase Transitions in Perovskites under XUV Irradiation: A Comparative Study of SrTiO3 and KTaO3
summary: We study ultrafast structural and electronic responses of strontium titanate and potassium tantalate to intense femtosecond irradiation using the XTANT3 multiscale code. It is found that at threshold doses of 0.7 eVatom in STO and 0.9 eVatom in KTO, a superionic state thermally forms with selective melting of the oxygen subsystem while metallic sublattices remain ordered. This state persists up to 1.6 eVatom STO and 1.5 eVatom KTO, above which complete disorder occurs. Analysis of the transient electronic density of states suggests that the B site d orbitals govern the divergent behaviour of the two materials: the compact Ti 3d orbitals in STO produce a narrow conduction band and large intraatomic exchange parameter, driving a transient ferromagnetic instability on 1 ps timescales, whereas the more spatially extended Ta 5d orbitals in KTO yield a broader conduction band and smaller exchange parameter, keeping KTO paramagnetic. These results suggest d orbital spatial extent as a structural parameter that influences phase transition sequences, and magnetic response under extreme electronic excitation, with implications for the ultrafast optical control of electronic and magnetic properties in perovskite based optoelectronic devices. Landau Devonshire analysis shows that irradiation at 0.3 eVatom transiently deepens the polar potential well in unstrained and strained STO and KTO, with the effect amplified approximately 2 fold in strained STO and 6 fold in strained KTO with respect to the unstrained cases.

AI.tldr: The paper uses the XTANT3 multiscale code to study ultrafast structural and electronic responses of strontium titanate (STO) and potassium tantalate (KTO) to intense femtosecond irradiation. It finds threshold doses for superionic state formation with selective oxygen sublattice melting, identifies the B-site d orbital spatial extent as the key factor driving divergent magnetic behavior (transient ferromagnetic instability in STO vs. paramagnetism in KTO), and shows via Landau-Devonshire analysis that irradiation transiently deepens the polar potential well, amplified in strained crystals.
AI.motivation: To understand how d orbital character governs phase transition sequences and magnetic responses in perovskite materials under extreme electronic excitation, with implications for ultrafast optical control of electronic and magnetic properties in perovskite-based optoelectronic devices.
AI.method: Multiscale simulation using the XTANT3 code on STO and KTO under intense femtosecond irradiation, combined with analysis of transient electronic density of states and Landau-Devonshire phenomenological analysis for polar potential well behavior in unstrained and strained configurations.
AI.result: STO forms a superionic state at 0.7 eV/atom (persisting to 1.6 eV/atom) and KTO at 0.9 eV/atom (persisting to 1.5 eV/atom), with selective oxygen sublattice melting. The compact Ti 3d orbitals in STO produce a narrow conduction band and large intraatomic exchange, driving transient ferromagnetism on ~1 ps timescales, whereas extended Ta 5d orbitals in KTO keep it paramagnetic. Irradiation at 0.3 eV/atom deepens the polar potential well, with ~2× amplification in strained STO and ~6× in strained KTO relative to unstrained cases.
AI.conclusion: The spatial extent of B-site d orbitals is a key structural parameter influencing phase transition sequences and magnetic response under extreme electronic excitation, offering routes for ultrafast optical control of electronic and magnetic properties in perovskite-based devices.

title: Ab initio High-Pressure Phase Diagrams of Al-Mg Alloys in the Low Solute Concentration Limit
summary: Binary alloy phase diagrams at high pressure are essential for understanding solidification and chemical partitioning in both engineered materials and planetary interiors, yet their experimental determination becomes increasingly challenging under extreme conditions. We apply a fully ab initio approach [J. Chem. Phys. 162, 184502 (2025)], based on density-functional theory, to compute the dilute-limit phase diagram of the Al-Mg system from ambient conditions up to 150 GPa. As a first step, we calculate the melting curves of pure fcc Al and pure hcp/bcc Mg, including the hcp-bcc phase boundary and triple point of Mg, all of which agree closely with available experimental data. The binary phase diagram is then constructed at both compositional extremes. On the Al-rich side, Mg consistently favours the liquid throughout the entire pressure range, with this preference strengthening monotonically under compression. On the Mg-rich side, Al partitions preferentially into the liquid at ambient pressure but undergoes a complete reversal above ~60 GPa, becoming solid-favouring as the Mg host transitions from hcp to bcc. This pressure-driven reversal inverts the topology of the Mg-rich coexistence field from a conventional downward-sloping to an upward-sloping phase boundary, and has direct implications for models of planetary differentiation and interior chemical stratification.

AI.tldr: A fully ab initio DFT-based approach is used to compute the dilute-limit phase diagram of the Al-Mg binary system from ambient pressure to 150 GPa. While Al favors the liquid on the Al-rich side throughout, Al partitioning on the Mg-rich side reverses above ~60 GPa from liquid-favoring to solid-favoring as Mg transitions from hcp to bcc, inverting the phase boundary topology with implications for planetary differentiation.
AI.motivation: Binary alloy phase diagrams at high pressure are essential for understanding solidification and chemical partitioning in engineered materials and planetary interiors, yet experimental determination under extreme conditions is increasingly challenging.
AI.method: A fully ab initio approach based on density-functional theory [J. Chem. Phys. 162, 184502 (2025)] is applied to compute the dilute-limit phase diagram of Al-Mg. First, melting curves of pure fcc Al and hcp/bcc Mg (including the hcp-bcc boundary and triple point of Mg) are calculated and validated against experiment. The binary phase diagram is then constructed at both compositional extremes.
AI.result: Pure-element melting curves agree closely with available experimental data. On the Al-rich side, Mg consistently prefers the liquid across the entire pressure range, with strengthening preference under compression. On the Mg-rich side, Al partitions into the liquid at ambient pressure but reverses above ~60 GPa, becoming solid-favoring as the Mg host transitions from hcp to bcc, inverting the coexistence field topology from downward-sloping to upward-sloping.
AI.conclusion: The pressure-driven partitioning reversal in the Mg-rich Al-Mg system has direct implications for models of planetary differentiation and interior chemical stratification.

title: Polaron-mediated metal-insulator transition and proton conduction in hydrogenated nickelate perovskites
summary: Nickel-based perovskites, owing to their spontaneous hydrogen uptake and the dramatic increase in resistivity upon hydrogenation, have emerged as promising candidates for proton-conducting fuel cell electrolytes. However, the mechanism of the hydrogen-induced metal-insulator transition (MIT) in rare-earth nickelates remains under debate, particularly regarding whether the doped electrons occupy Ni e$_g$ states or O 2p ligand hole states. Here, we reveal a comprehensive MIT mechanism using first-principles calculations on NdNiO$_3$: the electrons introduced by hydrogen doping occupy the O 2p ligand hole states of the Ni-O hybridized d$_8$L configuration, promoting electron-polaron formation. The resulting electron polarons, together with proton polarons, weaken the Ni-O hybridization and thereby drive the originally itinerant Ni e$_g$ electrons toward localization. This generates a local d8 (t$_{2g}$$^6$e$_g$$^2$) electronic configuration, leading to a Mott transition. In addition, we also find that compared with NdNiO$_3$, SmNiO$_3$ with a smaller A-site ionic radius more readily absorbs hydrogen but exhibits weaker proton diffusion capability. Hydrogenation promotes proton permeation along the [001] direction via the intraoctahedral transfer, whereas the overall proton diffusivity is reduced. These results provide guidance for experimental screening of strongly correlated oxides as electrolyte materials and offer theoretical insights for enhancing proton conductivity in rare-earth nickelates.

AI.tldr: Using first-principles calculations on NdNiO3, the authors reveal the microscopic mechanism of hydrogen-induced metal-insulator transition: hydrogen-doping electrons occupy O 2p ligand hole states of the Ni-O hybridized d8L configuration, forming electron polarons that, together with proton polarons, weaken Ni-O hybridization and drive Ni eg electrons toward localization, producing a local d8 configuration and a Mott transition. They also compare NdNiO3 and SmNiO3, finding that the smaller-A-site SmNiO3 absorbs hydrogen more readily but has weaker proton diffusion, with hydrogenation promoting proton permeation along [001] via intra-octahedral transfer while overall proton diffusivity is reduced.
AI.motivation: Rare-earth nickelate perovskites are promising proton-conducting fuel cell electrolytes due to spontaneous hydrogen uptake and a dramatic hydrogenation-induced resistivity increase, but the mechanism of the hydrogen-induced metal-insulator transition remains debated—specifically whether doped electrons occupy Ni eg states or O 2p ligand hole states. This question must be resolved to guide experimental screening and proton conductivity enhancement.
AI.method: First-principles calculations based on density functional theory were performed on NdNiO3 to examine the electronic structure and hydrogenation behavior. The electron occupation, polaron formation, and Ni-O hybridization changes upon hydrogen doping were analyzed, and a comparative study between NdNiO3 and SmNiO3 (differing in A-site ionic radius) was conducted for hydrogen absorption and proton diffusion properties, including proton permeation pathways along the [001] direction.
AI.result: Hydrogen-doping electrons occupy the O 2p ligand hole states of the Ni-O hybridized d8L configuration, promoting electron-polaron formation. These electron polarons and proton polarons weaken Ni-O hybridization, driving Ni eg electrons toward localization and producing a local d8 configuration that induces a Mott transition. SmNiO3, with a smaller A-site ionic radius, more readily absorbs hydrogen but exhibits weaker proton diffusion capability. Hydrogenation promotes proton permeation along [001] via intra-octahedral transfer, yet the overall proton diffusivity is reduced.
AI.conclusion: The comprehensive MIT mechanism resolves the long-standing debate by showing that hydrogen-induced electrons occupy O 2p ligand hole states (not Ni eg states), triggering polaron-driven Mott localization. The comparative findings on A-site ionic radius effects provide practical guidance for experimental screening of strongly correlated oxides as electrolyte materials and theoretical insights for enhancing proton conductivity in rare-earth nickelates.

title: Second-Harmonic Imaging of Magnetic Domains in Thin Film Hematite
comment: 26 pages, 13 figures; First two authors contributed equally to this work
summary: Hematite is an antiferromagnetic oxide and candidate altermagnetic insulator whose Néel order reorients from an easy-axis to an easy-plane phase at the Morin transition. Interpreting altermagnetic transport and symmetry sensitive optical responses requires knowledge of the Néel vector orientation relative to the crystal axes and of the domain structure within the probed device. Here, we show that polarization-resolved second-harmonic generation (SHG) microscopy resolves magnetic symmetry and domains in epitaxial (0001)-oriented hematite films. Across the Morin temperature, the SHG polarization anisotropy evolves from an approximately sixfold pattern consistent with the easy-axis orientation to pronounced twofold patterns consistent with the easy-plane orientation. A symmetry analysis based on magnetic-dipole and electric-quadrupole contributions reproduces this evolution. Importantly, the interference between SHG amplitudes that are odd and even under reversal of the magnetic order renders opposite Néel-vector orientations optically distinguishable. Consistently, opposite directions of an applied in-plane magnetic field produce distinct SHG responses in our experiments. Using this magnetic contrast, we image micrometer-scale domains, their reorganization across the Morin transition, and their reconfiguration under magnetic and thermal cycling, including a remanent change after cycling through the spin-flop transition. These results establish SHG microscopy as a local probe of magnetic symmetry, Néel-vector orientation, and domain evolution in hematite films.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that polarization-resolved second-harmonic generation (SHG) microscopy can resolve magnetic symmetry, Néel-vector orientation, and magnetic domain structure in epitaxial (0001)-oriented hematite films across the Morin transition, providing a local probe for altermagnetic order in this candidate altermagnetic insulator.
AI.motivation: Interpreting altermagnetic transport and symmetry-sensitive optical responses in hematite requires knowledge of the Néel vector orientation relative to crystal axes and the domain structure within the probed device, which has been missing.
AI.method: Polarization-resolved second-harmonic generation (SHG) microscopy combined with a symmetry analysis based on magnetic-dipole and electric-quadrupole contributions is used to probe epitaxial (0001)-oriented hematite films across the Morin transition temperature.
AI.result: SHG polarization anisotropy evolves from a sixfold pattern (easy-axis phase) to twofold patterns (easy-plane phase) across the Morin transition. Interference between SHG amplitudes odd and even under magnetic-order reversal makes opposite Néel-vector orientations optically distinguishable, enabling imaging of micrometer-scale domains and their reconfiguration under magnetic/thermal cycling.
AI.conclusion: SHG microscopy establishes itself as a local probe of magnetic symmetry, Néel-vector orientation, and domain evolution in hematite films, with potential implications for altermagnetic device characterization.

title: GRADAR: orientation-map-driven detection and ranking of grains for targeted two-beam electron channeling contrast imaging
summary: Electron channeling contrast imaging (ECCI) resolves individual dislocations in bulk samples, but only when the imaged grain is held in a two-beam diffraction condition to well under half a degree. In a polycrystal it must be re-established grain by grain, and every published workflow we are aware of chooses the grain first and solves the stage for that orientation. This paper treats the inverse problem: nominate one reflection family and a stage envelope, and determine which grains of an EBSD-mapped polycrystal can reach that family's two-beam condition, a question posed in 2019 and open since. At fixed tilt $t$, stage rotation sweeps the incident beam around a cone of half-angle $t$ in each grain's crystal frame, and a family with Bragg angle $θ_B$ is reachable exactly when one of its plane normals lies within $(t + θ_B)$ of the specimen surface. On a measured 163-grain austenitic stainless steel map at 20 kV, {111} reachability rises from 38.7% at 7 deg tilt to 77.3% at 15 deg; {220} and {311} already reach 79.8% and 91.4% at 7 deg. Ranking survivors by predicted darkness alone is wrong: same-family candidates are equivalent with respect to their own band at exact Bragg incidence, and the darkest tend to lie closest to rival-band Bragg conditions. GRADAR therefore ranks darkest-clean, gating every candidate on a minimum clearance from all rivals, and returns a dial-ready stage move per selected grain. Because the beam moves only ~0.12 deg per degree of stage rotation at 7 deg tilt, an ordinary rotation stage sets the selected condition to better than 0.1 deg. The predicted sweep is checked against the AstroECP dataset's published silicon precession series: simulated and measured traces agree at r = 0.84, and the measured intensity is dark at all 16 predicted two-beam edges. Per-grain polycrystal validation is deferred to a companion study.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces GRADAR, a workflow that solves the inverse problem in electron channeling contrast imaging (ECCI): given a reflection family and a stage envelope, it determines which grains of an EBSD-mapped polycrystal can reach the two-beam diffraction condition, then ranks them by "darkest-clean" criteria and returns dial-ready stage moves.
AI.motivation: ECCI requires a two-beam diffraction condition to within a fraction of a degree, and in polycrystals this condition must be re-established grain by grain. Existing workflows choose the grain first and solve for the stage. A question posed in 2019—given a reflection family and stage envelope, which grains can reach the two-beam condition—remained open until now.
AI.method: The approach treats the inverse problem: at fixed tilt t, stage rotation sweeps the incident beam around a cone of half-angle t in each grain's crystal frame. A family with Bragg angle θ_B is reachable exactly when one of its plane normals lies within (t + θ_B) of the specimen surface. GRADAR ranks candidates by "darkest-clean": gating every candidate on a minimum clearance from rival Bragg conditions, then returns a dial-ready stage move per selected grain.
AI.result: On a measured 163-grain austenitic stainless steel map at 20 kV, {111} reachability rises from 38.7% at 7° tilt to 77.3% at 15°; {220} and {311} already reach 79.8% and 91.4% at 7°. The predicted sweep was validated against the AstroECP dataset's silicon precession series: simulated and measured traces agree at r=0.84, and measured intensity is dark at all 16 predicted two-beam edges.
AI.conclusion: GRADAR provides a practical, dial-ready solution to the inverse ECCI reachability problem in polycrystals. It correctly predicts two-beam edges (validated on silicon) and is ready for per-grain polycrystal validation in a companion study.

title: Magnetically tunable symmetry-enforced nodal lines producing huge anomalous Hall conductivity in altermagnetic $α$-MnTe
summary: Altermagnetic $α$-MnTe exhibits huge anomalous Hall conductivity (AHC) up to room-temperature together with weak ferromagnetism arising from spin and orbital polarizations. We clarify the origin of the large value of the AHC by identifying two sets of distinct symmetry-enforced nodal lines in the valence bands with Mn character, located at $k_z=0$ and $k_z=\fracπ{c}$, protected by mirror symmetry $M_z$ and glide symmetry $G_z = \{M_z\,|\,0,0,\tfrac{c}{2}\}$, respectively. Both nodal lines are energy-dependent with an approximate C$_6$ symmetry, which is reduced to an exact C$_2$ symmetry due to the presence of the Néel vector. The highest valence band exhibits a Mexican-hat dispersion, whereas the second-highest valence band exhibits an inverted Mexican-hat dispersion, with nodal lines at the crossing between the two bands. Within first-principles accuracy, we demonstrate that these nodal lines give rise to the large AHC observed experimentally and exhibit a strong interplay with the weak ferromagnetism. We further show that even a small spin canting strongly modifies the nodal lines and the AHC, making them both magnetically tunable. By disentangling the altermagnetic and ferromagnetic contributions to the AHC, the altermagnetic contribution dominates at small canting angles, while the ferromagnetic contribution becomes sizeable for larger values. Using linear dichroism in angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy, we show a signature of the nodal line at the border of the Brillouin zone.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies two sets of symmetry-enforced nodal lines in the valence bands of altermagnetic α-MnTe, protected by mirror and glide symmetries, which give rise to the experimentally observed large anomalous Hall conductivity up to room temperature. The nodal lines are magnetically tunable through spin canting, and the authors disentangle altermagnetic and ferromagnetic contributions to the AHC.
AI.motivation: To clarify the microscopic origin of the huge anomalous Hall conductivity (AHC) observed in altermagnetic α-MnTe up to room temperature, which coexists with weak ferromagnetism.
AI.method: First-principles calculations identifying symmetry-enforced nodal lines (protected by M_z mirror and G_z glide symmetries) in the Mn-character valence bands, analysis of their energy-dependent dispersion with C6/C2 symmetry, decomposition of altermagnetic vs. ferromagnetic AHC contributions, and linear dichroism angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) to probe nodal-line signatures.
AI.result: Two sets of nodal lines at k_z=0 and k_z=π/c, protected by mirror and glide symmetries respectively, produce large AHC consistent with experiment. Small spin canting strongly modifies the nodal lines and AHC, making them magnetically tunable. The altermagnetic contribution dominates at small canting angles, while ferromagnetic contribution becomes sizeable at larger angles. ARPES confirms a nodal-line signature at the Brillouin zone border.
AI.conclusion: The large AHC in α-MnTe originates from symmetry-enforced nodal lines in the Mn-character valence bands, whose magnetic tunability via spin canting provides a path to control transport properties in altermagnets.

title: Real-time dynamics of the two-step charge-density-wave transition in bulk 1T-TaS$_2$
summary: The charge-density wave (CDW) of bulk 1T-TaS2 is built from Star-of-David (SoD) clusters tiling a sqrt{13} x sqrt{13} superlattice, and it melts through a two-step sequence accompanied by order-of-magnitude changes in resistivity. Whether these steps proceed by collapse of the SoD amplitude or by rearrangement of the SoD lattice has remained unresolved, because the relevant dynamics occur on length and time scales beyond the reach of ab initio molecular dynamics. Here we follow the CDW transitions in real time using a machine-learning force field trained on first-principles data, giving access to 1404-atom supercells over 5 ns. The two steps are mechanistically distinct. Above 200 K, SoD clusters translate coherently by transiently dissolving and re-forming about shifted centers, a deformation-formation process that preserves the local SoD amplitude while randomizing the interlayer stacking order and nucleating domain walls. Only near 350 K does the SoD distortion itself collapse. These results provide microscopic support for the recently proposed two-step model of the CDW transition and offer a framework for interpreting light-induced hidden phases and cavity-modified transition temperatures in 1T-TaS2.

title: Revealing Intrinsic Anisotropy of Collective Magnetic Excitations in Twinned Crystals of a Kitaev-Heisenberg Quantum Magnet
summary: Quantum magnets with competing interactions often emerge from delicate balances among microscopic parameters, making it essential to disentangle intrinsic spin dynamics from extrinsic disorder effects. Here, we introduce a multimodal optical approach combining magneto-infrared spectroscopy with domain-resolved micro-Raman spectroscopy at high magnetic fields to reconstruct the intrinsic magnetic excitation spectrum of twinned crystals of the Kitaev-Heisenberg quantum magnet Na$_3$Co$_2$SbO$_6$. Far-infrared spectroscopy reveals multiple field-tunable magnetic excitations, but the intrinsic response is obscured by replica features arising from twin domains. By correlating magneto-infrared and domain-resolved Raman spectra, we isolate the single-domain magnon response and uncover a pronounced twofold in-plane magnon anisotropy. This anisotropy far exceeds that expected from the measured in-plane g-factor anisotropy and is instead dominated by anisotropic bond-dependent exchange interactions. By unifying high-field, high-resolution and spatially selective optical probes, our work establishes a broadly applicable framework for revealing intrinsic spin dynamics and constraining the spin Hamiltonian in multidomain quantum magnets.
